full_text_sections.full_text: Diagnostic Preparedness and Biosafety Measures for Hantavirus Infections in Clinical Laboratories: A Systematic Review Journal Name: Annals of Medical and Health Research: An International Journal DOI: https://doi.org/10.51470/ARMHR.2026.5.1.104 Keywords: Hantavirus, laboratory preparedness, biosafety, molecular diagnosis, serological diagnosis, One Health, surveillance, Philippines Abstract Background: Hantavirus infections are potentially severe zoonotic diseases whose effective laboratory management requires timely clinical recognition, reliable diagnostic testing, appropriate biosafety practices, and surveillance of animal reservoirs. In the Philippines, evidence of human exposure and hantavirus circulation in wildlife exists, but contemporary information on hantavirus-specific diagnostic and biosafety preparedness remains limited. Methods: This systematic review evaluated evidence on hantavirus epidemiology, clinical recognition, laboratory diagnosis, reservoir surveillance, occupational exposure, and biosafety, with particular emphasis on implications for Philippine clinical laboratories. PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, and supplementary sources were searched. Of 304 records initially identified, 18 studies met the eligibility criteria. Because of substantial heterogeneity in study designs, populations, diagnostic approaches, and outcomes, findings were synthesized narratively and thematically. Results: Philippine evidence demonstrated 6.1% hantavirus antibody prevalence among 461 asymptomatic participants and molecular detection of Quezon virus in local wildlife. International studies demonstrated that hantavirus infection may be clinically misrecognized, including as dengue, and severe HPS was associated with substantial mortality. Molecular diagnostic studies showed that RT-qPCR can facilitate early detection, with one study reporting 94.9% sensitivity and 100% specificity. Serological and molecular methods were complementary, while reservoir studies demonstrated considerable hantavirus diversity. Occupational investigations documented laboratory-associated infections and highlighted aerosol exposure, infected animals, and potentially infectious specimens as important biosafety risks. Philippine studies demonstrated existing biosafety training capacity but identified broader gaps in biorisk management and pathogen-specific preparedness. Conclusion: Evidence of human exposure and wildlife-associated hantavirus circulation supports strengthened preparedness in the Philippines. A risk-based, tiered, and One Health approach integrating clinical recognition, serological and molecular testing, specimen-referral systems, quality assurance, biosafety training, occupational protection, and human–animal surveillance is warranted. Contemporary Philippine studies are needed to define current exposure, circulating viruses, and laboratory readiness. INTRODUCTION Hantaviruses are enveloped, negative-sense, single-stranded RNA viruses of the family Hantaviridae that are maintained primarily in rodent and other small-mammal reservoirs and transmitted to humans mainly through inhalation of aerosolized virus-contaminated urine, feces, or saliva [1]. Medically important hantaviruses cause two major clinical syndromes: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), occurring predominantly in Europe and Asia, and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) or hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), reported mainly in the Americas [2, 3]. The potentially severe clinical course of these infections makes early laboratory recognition and appropriate biosafety practices essential [4]. Laboratory assessment of hantavirus infection relies principally on serological and molecular methods [5]. Detection of hantavirus-specific IgM and IgG antibodies using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISA) is widely employed, while reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) enables detection of viral RNA, particularly during the acute phase [2]. Immunofluorescence, immunoblotting, neutralization assays, and immunohistochemistry may provide supplementary or confirmatory evidence [6]. The effectiveness of hantavirus diagnosis depends not only on the analytical performance of serological and molecular assays but also on the broader laboratory system in which testing occurs [7]. Essential components include appropriate laboratory infrastructure, trained personnel, early recognition and notification of suspected cases, safe specimen collection and transport, functional referral pathways to authorized reference laboratories, and quality-assurance procedures that support reliable and timely results [8]. Diagnostic preparedness must therefore be accompanied by appropriate biosafety and biorisk-management measures to protect laboratory personnel, prevent laboratory-associated transmission, and ensure that testing can be performed safely and reliably [9]. Laboratory personnel may encounter potentially infectious clinical specimens before hantavirus infection is recognized, creating occupational risks from aerosol-generating procedures, accidental percutaneous inoculation, mucous-membrane exposure, and contamination of work surfaces [10]. Risk-based precautions include appropriate personal protective equipment, biological safety cabinets, safe centrifugation, specimen inactivation where appropriate, decontamination, waste management, exposure-response procedures, and higher containment for activities involving propagation or concentration of live virus [11]. These measures are particularly important in laboratories with limited experience handling uncommon or emerging zoonotic pathogens, where agent-specific training, documented risk assessment, competency verification, and access to expert or reference-laboratory support may be limited [9]. At the population level, hantavirus infection remains an important zoonotic and public-health concern, with transmission shaped by rodent abundance, occupational and recreational exposure, climatic variability, urbanization, agricultural activity, and environmental disturbance [12]. Agricultural and forestry workers, military personnel, wildlife handlers, sanitation workers, and laboratory personnel may experience increased occupational exposure to hantaviruses through activities that bring them into contact with infected rodents, their excreta, contaminated environments, or potentially infectious specimens [13]. A recent global review reported that hantavirus seroprevalence among several occupational populations exceeded background population levels, emphasizing the importance of integrated surveillance, prevention, and occupational protection [3, 14]. These findings demonstrate that laboratory preparedness forms part of a broader One Health response connecting human health, reservoir surveillance, and environmental risk. In the Philippines, hantavirus remains underrecognized despite ecological conditions favorable to rodent-borne zoonoses and historical evidence of human exposure. Earlier seroepidemiological research demonstrated hantavirus antibodies among Filipino populations [15]. Philippine evidence indicates that hantavirus exposure has occurred in human populations, while studies of rodents and other wildlife suggest possible viral circulation in animal reservoirs. However, the available evidence remains limited by geographically restricted studies, incomplete surveillance, insufficient characterization of occupational and environmental risk factors, and constrained diagnostic capacity [15, 16]. The review emphasized the need for strengthened One Health surveillance, improved diagnostic capability, ecological monitoring, and occupational biosafety [17]. Evidence from other Asian countries, Europe, and the Americas is nevertheless essential because established diagnostic and biosafety systems internationally may provide approaches that can be adapted to Philippine and other resource-limited laboratory settings [18]. analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus infections are severe zoonoses needing timely recognition, reliable diagnostics, biosafety, and reservoir surveillance. Main directions: Limited Philippine data, clinical misrecognition, occupational aerosol risks, and a risk‑based One Health framework are highlighted. Current state: 6.1% seroprevalence, Quezon virus detection, RT‑qPCR ~95% sensitivity/100% specificity, and complementary serology/molecular methods are reported. Gaps: Only 18 heterogeneous studies limit conclusions; biorisk management and up‑to‑date exposure data are lacking. Future research: Philippines‑focused studies to map exposure, circulating strains, and lab readiness, and to apply a tiered One Health surveillance and biosafety approach.

papers.title: SARS, H1N1, EBOLA, COVID-19, MPOX, H5N1 AND HANTAVIRUS: IS HUMANITY ENTERING A NEW ERA OF PANDEMIC? IS TÜRKİYE PREPARED FOR THE NEXT GLOBAL OUTBREAK?
papers.abstract: The emergence and re-emergence of infectious diseases pose persistent challenges to global health security. Outbreaks such as severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS), influenza A(H1N1), Ebola virus disease, coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19), mpox, avian influenza A(H5N1), and hantavirus infections highlight the need for effective preparedness against emerging infectious threats. The concept of “Disease X” further emphasizes the importance of preparing for unknown pathogens that may cause future epidemics or pandemics. This study aimed to examine major infectious disease outbreaks and assess Türkiye’s preparedness for potential future global outbreaks. A descriptive review design was employed, based on a structured literature search and document analysis of scientific publications and institutional reports. The findings were organized and interpreted using a SWOT framework. The analysis identified healthcare infrastructure, intensive care capacity, digital health systems, and experience gained during the COVID-19 pandemic as potential strengths. However, challenges related to healthcare workforce capacity, zoonotic disease surveillance, public health literacy, coordination across human, animal, and environmental health sectors, and dependence on external sources for certain biotechnological products may constrain preparedness. Climate change, environmental disruption, international travel, migration, and global trade were identified as factors that may influence the emergence and spread of infectious diseases. Strengthening integrated surveillance and early warning systems, improving intersectoral coordination through the One Health approach, enhancing domestic vaccine and diagnostic production capacity, and expanding community-based public health education may help improve Türkiye’s preparedness for future outbreaks. These findings highlight the importance of sustained, multisectoral preparedness for emerging infectious disease threats.

Outbreaks such as severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS), influenza A(H1N1), Ebola virus disease, coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19), mpox, avian influenza A(H5N1), and hantavirus infections highlight the need for effective preparedness against emerging infectious threats. The concept of “Disease X” further emphasizes the importance of preparing for unknown pathogens that may cause future epidemics or pandemics. This study aimed to examine major infectious disease outbreaks and assess Türkiye’s preparedness for potential future global outbreaks. A descriptive review design was employed, based on a structured literature search and document analysis of scientific publications and institutional reports. The findings were organized and interpreted using a SWOT framework. The analysis identified healthcare infrastructure, intensive care capacity, digital health systems, and experience gained during the COVID-19 pandemic as potential strengths. However, challenges related to healthcare workforce capacity, zoonotic disease surveillance, public health literacy, coordination across human, animal, and environmental health sectors, and dependence on external sources for certain biotechnological products may constrain preparedness. Climate change, environmental disruption, international travel, migration, and global trade were identified as factors that may influence the emergence and spread of infectious diseases. Strengthening integrated surveillance and early warning systems, improving intersectoral coordination through the One Health approach, enhancing domestic vaccine and diagnostic production capacity, and expanding community-based public health education may help improve Türkiye’s preparedness for future outbreaks. These findings highlight the importance of sustained, multisectoral preparedness for emerging infectious disease threats.

Keywords: One Health, Pandemic preparedness, Turkish healthcare system, Zoonotic diseases Received: June 11, 2026 Accepted: October 16, 2026 1. Introduction Emerging and re-emerging infectious diseases continue to challenge global health security, demonstrating the need for sustained preparedness beyond individual epidemic events. Outbreaks of severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS), influenza A(H1N1), Ebola virus disease, and coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19), together with renewed concerns about avian influenza A(H5N1) and hantavirus infections, illustrate the diverse and evolving nature of infectious disease threats. The risk of future outbreaks is shaped by interconnected factors, including environmental change, biodiversity loss, urbanization, international travel, and increased interactions between humans, animals, and their shared environments. Consequently, pandemic preparedness requires more than adequate clinical capacity; it Int. J. of Health Serv. Res. and Policy (2026) 11(3):270-280 https://doi.org/10.33457/ijhsrp.1969304 271 also depends on effective surveillance, timely risk assessment, intersectoral coordination, and international cooperation. The COVID-19 pandemic exposed substantial differences in countries’ capacities to prevent, detect, and respond to public health emergencies, reinforcing the importance of strengthening preparedness at both national and global levels. The adoption of the World Health Organization’s Pandemic Agreement in 2025 further underscored international efforts to improve pandemic prevention, preparedness, and response [1]. The emergence of zoonotic diseases is closely associated with ecological and environmental changes that alter interactions among humans, wildlife, and domestic animals. Evidence indicates that zoonotic host diversity can increase in human-dominated ecosystems, while climate change may alter opportunities for viral transmission between species [2], [3]. These findings reinforce the importance of understanding infectious disease emergence through an integrated perspective rather than considering human health in isolation. The One Health approach provides a framework for addressing the interconnectedness of human, animal, and environmental health and has been increasingly emphasized in research on emerging infectious diseases and pandemic preparedness [4], [5]. Against this background, this study examines major infectious disease outbreaks with global public health implications, considers factors that may contribute to future pandemic risks, and assesses Türkiye’s preparedness for potential future outbreaks using a SWOT analysis framework. 2. Materials and Methods 2.1. Research Type This study employed a descriptive review design based on a structured literature search and document analysis. The review examined scientific publications and official institutional documents concerning major infectious disease outbreaks, zoonotic risks, and pandemic preparedness, with particular emphasis on Türkiye’s healthcare system. The review was not designed as a systematic review; rather, it aimed to synthesize relevant documentary evidence and interpret the findings using a SWOT framework. The analysis focused on identifying reported healthcare capacities, structural challenges, opportunities for improvement, and potential threats to Türkiye’s preparedness for future global outbreaks. 2.2. Data Sources This study was based exclusively on secondary sources and did not involve primary data collection or direct interaction with human participants. The sources included scientific publications and official reports from the Republic of Türkiye Ministry of Health, the World Health Organization (WHO), the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), and the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC), as well as other relevant institutional documents and peer-reviewed publications. 2.3. Literature Search Strategy and Eligibility Criteria The review included scientific publications and official institutional documents addressing major infectious disease outbreaks, zoonotic risks, and pandemic preparedness, with particular emphasis on Türkiye’s healthcare system. Eligible sources were required to provide relevant information on disease emergence, outbreak management, surveillance, healthcare system capacity, or pandemic preparedness. Peer-reviewed articles, official reports, and relevant institutional documents were considered for inclusion. Duplicate records, sources with insufficient methodological information, and publications unrelated to the study objectives were excluded. The review focused on seven disease groups identified in the study title: SARS, influenza A(H1N1), Ebola virus disease, COVID-19, mpox, avian influenza A(H5N1), and hantavirus infections. Int. J. of Health Serv. Res. and Policy (2026) 11(3):270-280 https://doi.org/10.33457/ijhsrp.1969304 272 2.4. Document Review Procedure Data were collected through the examination of scientific publications and official institutional documents. The reviewed sources were assessed for information concerning disease characteristics, outbreak management, surveillance systems, healthcare infrastructure, and national and international pandemic preparedness. Relevant information was recorded and organized according to its relevance to the study objectives and the SWOT framework. No primary data collection instrument was used because the study relied exclusively on secondary sources. 2.5. Literature Search and Selection Process The literature search covered publications from 2002 to 2026. Sources were identified through searches of publications and reports issued by the Republic of Türkiye Ministry of Health, the YÖK National Thesis Center, TR Index (ULAKBİM), the TÜBİTAK ULAKBİM Medical Database, DergiPark, PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Türk Medline, and Google Scholar. Search terms included “pandemic preparedness,” “zoonotic diseases,” “One Health,” “Turkish healthcare system,” “SARS,” “H1N1,” “Ebola,” “COVID-19,” “Mpox,” “H5N1,” and “Hantavirus.” These terms were used individually and in combination, where appropriate. Records were assessed for relevance to the study objectives, publication type, and contribution to the understanding of pandemic preparedness and zoonotic disease risks. Duplicate records, publications with insufficient methodological information, and sources unrelated to the research objectives were excluded. 2.6. Data Analysis The included documents were analyzed qualitatively using a descriptive approach. Relevant information concerning Türkiye’s preparedness for emerging infectious diseases and future pandemics was identified and organized according to the study objectives. The extracted information was classified into four SWOT categories: strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats. Strengths and weaknesses represented reported internal capacities and challenges of the healthcare and preparedness systems, whereas opportunities and threats represented external developments and conditions that could influence preparedness. The resulting categories were interpreted in relation to the documentary evidence reviewed. This approach provided the analytical basis for the SWOT findings presented in the Results section. 3. Results 3.1. SWOT Analysis for Türkiye 3.1.1 Strengths • Strengthened public health infrastructure and outbreak management experience following COVID-19 • Advanced laboratory capacity and widespread molecular diagnostic methods • Digital surveillance and infectious disease monitoring systems operated by the Ministry of Health • Experience gained in filiation and contact tracing practices • Extensive hospital network and high intensive care capacity • Increasing academic interest in the One Health approach • Improved emergency management capacity after COVID-19 • Strengthened vaccine and pharmaceutical logistics infrastructure Int. J. of Health Serv. Res. and Policy (2026) 11(3):270-280 https://doi.org/10.33457/ijhsrp.1969304 273 3.1.2 Weaknesses • Insufficient zoonotic disease surveillance systems • Deficiencies in rodent population control • Limited public awareness regarding zoonotic infections • Biosafety challenges in rural areas • Limited implementation of the One Health approach • Healthcare workforce shortages and burnout risks • Inadequate virus-specific national preparedness and emergency response plans 3.1.3 Opportunities • Increased healthcare investments after COVID-19 • Expanding collaborations with WHO and international organizations • Development of artificial intelligence–supported epidemiological surveillance systems • Increasing cooperation between universities and the Ministry of Health • Potential for developing digital early warning systems • Advancements in domestic vaccine and biotechnology production capacity • Integration potential of the One Health approach into national health policies • Increasing academic research on zoonotic diseases • Expansion of community-based public health education programs • Opportunities for integration among veterinary medicine, environmental health, and human health sectors 3.1.4 Threats • Increasing rodent populations associated with climate change • Emergence of new zoonotic diseases • Increased transmission risks associated with global travel and trade • Environmental hygiene problems in rural areas • Increased rodent exposure risks in agricultural settings • Delayed diagnosis and intervention in rare infectious diseases • Potential burden of global outbreaks on the healthcare system • Biological risks associated with international food trade and logistics • Misinformation and infodemic-related risks 4. Historical Development of Pandemic and Increasing Global Risk 4.1. SARS (2002-2003) Severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) emerged in southern China in 2002 and spread internationally, demonstrating how rapidly an emerging infectious disease can cross national borders through international travel. The outbreak highlighted the importance of early case detection, infection prevention and control, contact tracing, and coordinated international surveillance. The outbreak was brought under control in 2003 following coordinated international surveillance and public health interventions, highlighting the importance of early detection, case identification, and infection control in containing emerging infectious diseases [6]. 4.2. Influenza A/H1N1 (Swine Flu) Pandemic (2009) Influenza A/H1N1 was a global influenza pandemic that emerged in 2009. Commonly referred to as “swine flu” because it was initially identified in pigs, the disease rapidly evolved into a global Int. J. of Health Serv. Res. and Policy (2026) 11(3):270-280 https://doi.org/10.33457/ijhsrp.1969304 274 pandemic due to its high transmissibility, despite having a lower mortality rate compared with SARS. Particularly high infection rates among young adults attracted considerable attention. Following the H1N1 pandemic, many countries updated their pandemic preparedness plans, strengthened influenza surveillance systems, and increased vaccine production capacity [7]. Today, H1N1 remains among the circulating seasonal influenza strains and continues to be monitored as an important global public health concern. WHO officially declared the H1N1 outbreak a pandemic in 2009 [7]. 4.3. Ebola Virus Disease Ebola virus disease is considered one of the deadliest viral hemorrhagic fevers of the modern era due to its high mortality rate and devastating impact on healthcare systems. The 2014–2016 West African outbreak caused not only severe health consequences but also major economic and social destruction. During the outbreak, infection among healthcare workers highlighted the critical importance of infection prevention and control measures [8]. Ebola outbreaks contributed significantly to strengthening the concept of global health security by promoting the development of early diagnosis systems, contact tracing, isolation practices, field epidemiology, and international coordination mechanisms. Although the development of effective vaccines represents substantial progress, Ebola remains a closely monitored infectious disease due to persistent zoonotic transmission risks and fragile healthcare infrastructures in parts of Africa [8]. 4.4. Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) Pandemic COVID-19 became the largest global health crisis of the modern era. The collapse of healthcare systems, shortages in intensive care capacity, disruptions in global supply chains, and vaccine inequities deepened the global consequences of the pandemic. COVID-19 demonstrated that healthcare systems should not be evaluated solely on the basis of hospital capacity. It also revealed the critical importance of data management, digital health technologies, early warning systems, and scientific coordination capacity [9]. 4.5. Mpox (Monkeypox) Mpox is a zoonotic viral infection that has become an important global health concern due to its increasing international spread in recent years. The 2022 global outbreak demonstrated that the disease was not limited to the African continent and could rapidly spread across regions through international travel and close-contact networks. During this period, contact tracing, isolation practices, and community-based awareness campaigns played critical roles in infection control [10]. The mpox outbreak also tested the preparedness of global healthcare systems against emerging infections in the post-COVID-19 era. Although the mortality rate of mpox is lower than that of Ebola or SARS, the disease remains a major public health concern because of its rapid transmission potential and burden on healthcare systems. In particular, insufficient surveillance systems and limited healthcare access in endemic African regions increase the risk of future outbreaks [10]. 4.6. Avian Influenza A/H5N1 (Bird Flu) The H5N1 influenza virus is among the highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) viruses and constitutes a major zoonotic threat with global transmission potential through bird populations. Although human infections are relatively rare, the virus causes major public health concerns because of its high mortality rate when transmission occurs. Migratory waterfowl, which serve as the primary reservoirs of the virus, play a critical role in intercontinental spread [11]. In recent years, the ability of H5N1 to infect certain mammalian species in addition to birds has been considered a serious warning regarding the virus’s adaptive capacity. This has raised concerns about the potential emergence of a new Int. J. of Health Serv. Res. and Policy (2026) 11(3):270-280 https://doi.org/10.33457/ijhsrp.1969304 275 influenza pandemic through mutations enabling human-to-human transmission. Consequently, WHO and other international health organizations continue to monitor H5N1 as a virus with high pandemic potential [11]. 4.7. Hantavirus Infection Hantaviruses are zoonotic viruses belonging to the Hantaviridae family. These viruses naturally circulate among rodents and are transmitted to humans through contact with infected rodent urine, feces, or saliva. Transmission generally occurs via aerosolized particles, particularly in rural areas and environments with dense rodent populations. papers.title: Cuadro clínico y eventos inmunológicos del síndrome cardiopulmonar por variantes Sudamericanas de Hantavirus: revisión sistemática
papers.abstract: Objetivo. Analizar los mecanismos inmunopatológicos implicados en el desarrollo del HCPS y su correlación con la severidad de las manifestaciones clínicas de las variantes sudamericanas. Métodos. Se realizó una revisión sistemática de la literatura científica sobre la inmunopatogenia de hantavirus sudamericanos bajo los lineamientos PRISMA 2020. Desarrollo. Las variantes de Hantavirus en Bolivia (ANDV, RIOMV y LNV) desencadenan el HCPS. El virus infecta el endotelio sin destruirlo directamente. La variante AND evade la respuesta innata acumulando alta carga viral, mientras RIOMV hiperestimula macrófagos y perfil Th1/Th17. Esto desregula la permeabilidad capilar, causando edema pulmonar no cardiogénico y shock cardiogénico. Conclusiones. El síndrome es una enfermedad inmunomediada donde la severidad depende de la variante genética. El daño tisular no es lítico, sino el resultado de una respuesta inmune descontrolada y una tormenta de citocinas. Comprender esta inmunopatogenia es crucial para diseñar terapias dirigidas a regular la inflamación sistémica.

papers.full_text: 100 G MB julio-diciembre 2026 Gac Med Bol 2026; 49(2): Lilian Verduguez-Orellana1a, Aleida Verduguez-Orellana1,2b Clinical features and immunological events of cardiopulmonary syndrome caused by South American Hantavirus variants: a systematic review Cuadro clínico y eventos inmunológicos del síndrome cardiopulmonar por variantes Sudamericanas de Hantavirus: revisión sistemática DOI: https://doi.org/10.47993/gmb.v49i2.1344 Check for updates En Bolivia circulan las variantes ANDV, RIOMV y LNV, cuya severidad clínica difiere. Objetivo: Analizar los mecanismos inmunopatológicos del síndrome cardiopulmonar por Hantavirus (HCPS) y su relación con la gravedad de las variantes sudamericanas. Métodos: Revisión sistemática según la declaración PRISMA 2020. Resultados: El virus infecta el endotelio sin daño citopático directo. ANDV evade la respuesta innata acumulando alta carga viral; RIOMV hiperestimula macrófagos con perfil Th1/Th17; mientras que LNV induce una respuesta equilibrada con oportuna síntesis de interferón tipo I. Estas vías alteran la permeabilidad capilar pulmonar y cardíaca, causando edema pulmonar no cardiogénico y shock cardiogénico. Conclusión: El HCPS está mediado por la respuesta inmune y su severidad depende de la variante viral. El daño tisular deriva de una respuesta inmune descontrolada y tormenta de citocinas, por lo que comprender esta inmunopatogenia es esencial para diseñar terapias dirigidas, ya que, no se cuenta con un tratamiento específico. Palabras claves: choque cardiogénico, infecciones por hantavirus, síndrome de dificultad respiratoria del adulto, síndrome pulmonar por hantavirus, tormenta de citocinas. Resumen In Bolivia, the ANDV, RIOMV, and LNV variants circulate, differing in clinical severity. Objective: To analyze the immunopathogenic mechanisms of Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) and their relationship with the severity of South American variants. Methods: Systematic review following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Results: The virus infects the endothelium without direct cytopathic damage. ANDV evades the innate response, accumulating a high viral load; RIOMV hyperstimulates macrophages with a Th1/Th17 profile; whereas LNV induces a balanced response with timely type I interferon synthesis. These pathways alter pulmonary and cardiac capillary permeability, causing non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema and cardiogenic shock. Conclusion: HCPS is immune-mediated, and its severity depends on the viral variant. Tissue damage stems from an uncontrolled immune response and cytokine storm; thus, understanding this immunopathogenesis is essential to design targeted therapies, as no specific treatment is available. Keywords: cardiogenic shock, hantavirus infections, adult respiratory distress syndrome, hantavirus pulmonary syndrome, cytokine storm. Abstract 1Centro Universitario de Medicina Tropical (CUMETROP), Instituto de Investigaciones Biomédicas (IIBISMED), Facultad de Medicina, Universidad Mayor de San Simón, Cochabamba, Bolivia. 2Laboratorio de Radioinmunoensayo, Centro de Medicina Nuclear ahttps://orcid.org/0009-0006-3169-764X lilianverduguez@gmail.com bhttps://orcid.org/0000-0001-7896-9952 a.verduguez@umss.edu *Correspondencia: Aleida Verduguez Orellana Correo electrónico: a.verduguez@umss.edu Recibido el 30 de junio de 2026 Aceptado 16 de septiembre de 2026 https://doi.org/10.47993/gmb.v49i2.1344 L a severidad del Síndrome Cardiopulmonar por Hantavirus (HCPS), desde la perspectiva biológica, es causado por diferentes variantes de hantavirus, que circulan en la región de las américas; siendo la más severa la variante Andes (ANDV)1, 2. En cambio otras variantes tales como Laguna Negra (LNV), Río Mamoré (RIOMV), ocasionan un HCSP entre moderado y leve con mejor pronóstico de recuperación3,4. Desde la perspectiva clínica, el HCPS, como evento, inicia posterior a un período de incubación de unas 2 semanas en promedio4. La fase febril del HCPS inicia con síntomas inespecíficos como fiebre, cefalea, mialgias/artralgias, sintomatología gastrointestinal3,5 y ausencia de sintomatología del tracto respiratorio superior6, estos, aparecerán recién en la fase sindrómica. La fase cardiopulmonar inicia de manera súbita con disnea progresiva acompañada de tos, además de hipoxia severa, la cual se evidencia con cianosis peribucal y desaturación de pulso. Al tercer día el paciente presenta taquicardia e hipotensión3,7. La mitad de los afectados, desarrollan daño renal agudo y un tercio presenta shock. Es en esta fase donde ocurren la gran parte de los decesos3, 6. Los eventos inmunológicos implicados en el desencadenamiento del HCSP independientemente de la variante de hantavirus responsable de la infección, son complejos e interdependientes, con la participación de la inmunidad innata mediante las AR01 Artículos de Revisión Review Article 101 G MB julio-diciembre 2026 Gac Med Bol 2026; 49(2): células dendríticas y sus productos químicos próximas a las células endoteliales pulmonares, así como también la activación de la inmunidad adaptativa celular, principalmente de linfocitos CD8, complementadas con una desregulación de la respuesta inmune global caracterizada por una tormenta de citocinas4. El objetivo de la presente revisión es analizar los mecanismos inmunológicos que conducen al desarrollo del HCSP por la infección con las variantes de Hantavirus ANDV; RIOMV y LNV que circulan en el territorio boliviano y explicar desde esa perspectiva las manifestaciones clínicas que evidencian la presencia de este síndrome. Metodología Esta revisión sistemática se estructuró siguiendo los lineamientos de la declaración PRISMA 2020 y fue registrada en la plataforma internacional PROSPERO con el código CRD420261437203. Consultamos exhaustivamente las bases de datos PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase y Scopus para literatura publicada hasta junio de 2026. Para sistematizar la información, aplicamos una estrategia de búsqueda combinada mediante operadores booleanos (AND, OR) que integró términos MeSH, DeCS y palabras clave en texto libre: ("Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome"[Mesh] OR "Hantavirus"[Mesh] OR "Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome"[TiAb] OR "Andes virus"[TiAb] OR "Laguna Negra virus"[TiAb] OR "Rio Mamore virus"[TiAb]) AND ("Cytokine Storm"[Mesh] OR "Immunity, Innate"[Mesh] OR "Immunity, Cellular"[Mesh] OR "Capillary Permeability"[Mesh] OR "immunopathogenesis"[TiAb] OR "immune response"[TiAb] OR "Th1/Th17"[TiAb] OR "VEGF"[TiAb] OR "VE-cadherin"[TiAb]) AND ("South America"[Mesh] OR "Bolivia"[Mesh]). Se incluyo estudios observacionales, ensayos clínicos y modelos experimentales (in vitro e in vivo) enfocados en la inmunopatogenia de estas variantes sudamericanas y su relación con la gravedad clínica. Se excluyeron revisiones puramente narrativas, investigaciones ecológicas o mastozoológicas sin correlación biomédica y trabajos sobre hantavirus del Viejo Mundo. De los 1 585 registros iniciales, eliminamos 435 duplicados y evaluamos 1 150 mediante la lectura de título y resumen. Tras descartar 1 012 artículos irrelevantes, evaluamos el texto completo de 138 contribuciones, excluyendo 109 por deficiencias metodológicas o falta de datos inmunológicos específicos. Finalmente, seleccionamos 28 estudios de alta relevancia para la síntesis cualitativa; el flujo cuantitativo de selección se detalla en el diagrama PRISMA (Figura 1). Tanto el cribado de los registros como la valoración del riesgo de sesgo fueron ejecutados de manera independiente por dos investigadores, detallando la resolución de discrepancias mediante consenso o un tercer revisor. Para la evaluación del riesgo de sesgo, se midió la calidad de los diseños epidemiológicos mediante la Escala Newcastle- AR01 Figura 1. Diagrama de flujo PRISMA del proceso de selección. Elaboración propia. 102 G MB julio-diciembre 2026 Gac Med Bol 2026; 49(2): Ottawa (NOS), incluyendo trabajos con una puntuación ≥ 6 estrellas. En el caso de las investigaciones de ciencia básica, se empleó una lista de parámetros adaptada del Instituto Joanna Briggs (JBI), para constatar el control de variables en los modelos celulares y líneas endoteliales analizadas. Resultados Clínica de la infección por Hantavirus: variantes ANDV, LNV y RIOMV Los hantavirus, variantes RIOMV, LNV, ANDV (circulantes en el territorio boliviano), producen una sintomatología similar entre todos ellos, así como también con otras variantes que circulan en la región de las américas y únicamente se diferencian en cuanto a la severidad del cuadro clínico de la enfermedad que producen1,8. La infección, se inicia por la inhalación de aerosoles procedentes de las excreciones de roedores infectados por partículas virales del grupo de los hantavirus5. Posterior a un período de incubación variable de 9 a 30 días, sin ningún síntoma clínicamente identificable, posteriormente se inicia la fase prodrómica o febril, inespecífica caracterizada por la presencia de fiebre >38 oC, mialgias intensas generalmente en músculos largos, cefalea retroorbitaria y síntomas gastrointestinales como náuseas y/o vómitos y dolor abdominal, el cual suele ser muy intenso, sobre todo cuando la infección es ocasionada por la variante ANDV y puede llegar a confundirse con un cuadro de abdomen agudo y en ciertos casos se puede llegar a evidenciar petequias en región axilar y en extremidades; además son frecuentes las manifestaciones hemorrágicas como la hematuria, metrorragia o hemoptisis2,3,5,9. Durante este período, destaca la ausencia de síntomas del tracto respiratorio superior6. La etapa de transición crítica, comienza al segundo día de iniciada la sintomatología, cuando las variantes implicadas son RIOMV y LNV; en cambio recién inicia al tercer día en el caso de la variante ANDV; esta etapa comprende un período variable AR01 Clínica e inmunología del HCPS Figura 2. Patogénesis comparativa de tres variantes sudamericanas de Hantavirus a nivel del tracto respiratorio. Composición gráfica generada por IA en base a las referencias 1 a 10. Artículos de Revisión Review Article 103 G MB julio-diciembre 2026 Gac Med Bol 2026; 49(2): de entre 8 a 24 horas6,9, con el comienzo evidente de la fase cardiopulmonar marcada por la aparición súbita de tos seca, disnea, inicialmente leve que progresa rápidamente a grave, y taquipnea (>22 rpm) indicando hipoxia3,8, la misma que, en casos severos, habitualmente relacionados con la infección por la variante ANDV, se manifiesta con cianosis peribucal, además de retracción intercostal y crepitantes bibalares a la auscultación pulmonar7. Al cuarto día, se evidencia taquicardia (>100 lpm) e hipotensión3,5,9. Finalmente, se instaura un edema pulmonar no cardiogénico llevando a una insuficiencia respiratoria aguda y en un 33% de los casos, independientemente de la variante de Hantavirus implicada, se produce shock cardiogénico con resistencia vascular periférica normal con insuficiencia cardíaca congestiva aguda, causando así, la mayor parte de los decesos5,6,9. Los que sobreviven a la fase crítica pasan a la fase de convalecencia que se caracteriza por diuresis elevada, resolución del edema pulmonar en las siguientes 24 a 48 horas y retiro progresivo de la oxigenoterapia. La recuperación completa puede llevar hasta dos años2,5. Existe escasa información clínica específica, respecto a la infección por la variante RIOMV, y se señala que esta variante además de lo señalado anteriormente ocasiona hemorragia intraparenquimal en los dos hemisferios y hemorragia subaracnoidea junto a un cuadro clínico hepatomegalia y daño renal agudo al segundo día7. Por el contrario, en la infección por la variante LNV se evidencia una clínica con menor severidad y mayor incidencia de infecciones leves o subclínicas, con una carga viral baja y una letalidad menor al 20%3,10. Respecto a la variante ANDV, las evidencias clínicas adicionales señalan también la afección del sistema nervioso central con encefalitis acompañada de cefalea intensa y fotofobia11 y una letalidad cercana al 40%2. Infección por Hantavirus variantes sudamericanas y Respuesta inmune Las variantes sudamericanas de hantavirus, infectan las células endoteliales del tracto respiratorio, mediante su acoplamiento a las integrinas αvβ3 y αIIbβ3, alterando el proceso de señalización celular habitual para posibilitar la replicación viral masiva, pero sin ocasionar un efecto citopático directo4,13. La variante ANDV, infecta de la forma anteriormente descrita, vía las integrinas, además de las células epiteliales de los alvéolos respiratorios también a las células de las glándulas salivales humanas1,2,3. Tras su ingreso a la células, la maquinaria viral, mediante su proteína no estructural NSs, inhibe la respuesta inmune innata, por interacción con la proteína adaptadora celular MAVS (Mitochondrial Antiviral-Signaling Protein), bloqueando la producción de los interferones tipo I; al silenciar la producción de estos interferones, la maquinaria viral permite acumular altas cargas virales intracelulares14,15,16, que posteriormente ejercerán un efecto indirecto en el desencadenamiento del HCPS17. Esta evasión inicial de la respuesta inmune innata, además impacta tardíamente en el brazo adaptativo de la respuesta inmune, caracterizado por una desmedida expansión clonal de linfocitos T CD8+ citotóxicos hiperactivados, los cuales migran masivamente al endotelio pulmonar, donde inducen AR01 Figura 3. Fisiopatología del Síndrome Cardiopulmonar por Hantavirus (HCPS). Composición gráfica generada por IA en base a las referencias 4, 24-28. 104 G MB julio-diciembre 2026 Gac Med Bol 2026; 49(2): AR01 un daño tisular mediado por la acción de perforinas y citocinas proinflamatorias, desestabilizando las uniones intercelulares estrechas sin causar lisis celular directa18. A diferencia de los mecanismos disruptivos de la respuesta inmune empleados por la maquinaria viral de la variante ANDV, la variante RIOMV, una vez ingresada dentro las células endoteliales, promueve la hiperestimulación desregulada de la inmunidad innata a partir de la interacción del RNA viral con los receptores tipo Toll 3 y 7 (TLR-3/7) el RIG-I (Gen I inducible por ácido retinoico), generando una transcripción explosiva de las quimiocinas: RANTES, IP-10 y MCP-1 las cuales a su vez inducen el reclutamiento de monocitos y macrófagos alveolares de forma masiva19. Los monocitos/macrófagos, activan la enzima iNOS y liberan niveles nocivos de óxido nítrico y citocinas pirogénicas (TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6)20. A nivel de la respuesta inmune adaptativa, la hiperestimulación desregulada de la respuesta innata, distorsiona el microambiente linfoide, polarizando fuertemente la diferenciación de linfocitos T colaboradores (CD4+) hacia los perfiles efectores Th1 y Th1721. Mientras que la vía Th1 perpetúa el daño celular mediante la liberación sostenida de IFN-γ, el perfil Th17 exacerba el reclutamiento de neutrófilos y desestabiliza directamente la barrera endotelial pulmonar mediante la secreción de IL-1722. Esta sinergia inmunopatológica culmina en una disfunción endotelial profunda, aumento de la permeabilidad capilar y el cuadro grave de SCPH documentado en infecciones por RIOMV3,4,7. El mecanismo empleado por la variante LNV, a diferencia de las dos anteriores, una vez que ingresa a las células endoteliales del tracto respiratorio, es el de estimular un acoplamiento simétrico y controlado entre los componentes innato y adaptativo de la respuesta inmune23. La variante LNV no suprime eficazmente las vías de señalización de los receptores de reconocimiento de patrones (PRRs), permitiendo una síntesis oportuna de IFN Tipo I en las fases iniciales, posibilitando así, la limitación de la replicación microvascular temprana, impidiendo altas cargas virales en el parénquima pulmonar10. A nivel de la respuesta inmune adaptativa, las células dendríticas maduran en un microambiente inflamatorio controlado, favoreciendo una diferenciación linfocitaria T equilibrada eficiente y una rápida maduración de la inmunidad humoral4 (Figura 2). Discusión Síndrome cardiopulmonar por Hantavirus y desregulación de la respuesta inmune Clínicamente, el HCPS se origina después de un período variable de incubación viral post infección en función de la variante de Hantavirus implicada2-9; en cambio, los eventos inmunológicos desencadenantes de este síndrome, inician en la etapa temprana de la infección, a partir de la alteración de la integridad de la barrera endotelial, con lo cual se incrementa la permeabilidad vascular, que si bien no es aun clínicamente identificable, la misma, en la etapa sindrómica se verá mucho más incrementada como resultado de la tormenta de citocinas, que se denomina retroalimentación positiva en la afección de la permeabilidad4. La alteración de la integridad de la barrera endotelial, como ya se señaló previamente, responde a la interacción de las variantes de Hantavirus con las moléculas integrinas β3, presentes en las células endoteliales, esta interacción, produce la hipersensibilidad de las células endoteliales el VEGF (Factor de Crecimiento Endotelial Vascular, por sus siglas en inglés) y una inhibición de la capacidad de migración de las células endoteliales sobre vitronectina4,24. full_text_sections.full_text: 100 G MB julio-diciembre 2026 Gac Med Bol 2026; 49(2): Lilian Verduguez-Orellana1a, Aleida Verduguez-Orellana1,2b Clinical features and immunological events of cardiopulmonary syndrome caused by South American Hantavirus variants: a systematic review Cuadro clínico y eventos inmunológicos del síndrome cardiopulmonar por variantes Sudamericanas de Hantavirus: revisión sistemática DOI: https://doi.org/10.47993/gmb.v49i2.1344 Check for updates En Bolivia circulan las variantes ANDV, RIOMV y LNV, cuya severidad clínica difiere. Objetivo: Analizar los mecanismos inmunopatológicos del síndrome cardiopulmonar por Hantavirus (HCPS) y su relación con la gravedad de las variantes sudamericanas. Métodos: Revisión sistemática según la declaración PRISMA 2020. Resultados: El virus infecta el endotelio sin daño citopático directo. ANDV evade la respuesta innata acumulando alta carga viral; RIOMV hiperestimula macrófagos con perfil Th1/Th17; mientras que LNV induce una respuesta equilibrada con oportuna síntesis de interferón tipo I. Estas vías alteran la permeabilidad capilar pulmonar y cardíaca, causando edema pulmonar no cardiogénico y shock cardiogénico. Conclusión: El HCPS está mediado por la respuesta inmune y su severidad depende de la variante viral. El daño tisular deriva de una respuesta inmune descontrolada y tormenta de citocinas, por lo que comprender esta inmunopatogenia es esencial para diseñar terapias dirigidas, ya que, no se cuenta con un tratamiento específico. Palabras claves: choque cardiogénico, infecciones por hantavirus, síndrome de dificultad respiratoria del adulto, síndrome pulmonar por hantavirus, tormenta de citocinas. Resumen In Bolivia, the ANDV, RIOMV, and LNV variants circulate, differing in clinical severity. Objective: To analyze the immunopathogenic mechanisms of Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) and their relationship with the severity of South American variants. Methods: Systematic review following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Results: The virus infects the endothelium without direct cytopathic damage. ANDV evades the innate response, accumulating a high viral load; RIOMV hyperstimulates macrophages with a Th1/Th17 profile; whereas LNV induces a balanced response with timely type I interferon synthesis. These pathways alter pulmonary and cardiac capillary permeability, causing non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema and cardiogenic shock. Conclusion: HCPS is immune-mediated, and its severity depends on the viral variant. Tissue damage stems from an uncontrolled immune response and cytokine storm; thus, understanding this immunopathogenesis is essential to design targeted therapies, as no specific treatment is available. Keywords: cardiogenic shock, hantavirus infections, adult respiratory distress syndrome, hantavirus pulmonary syndrome, cytokine storm. Abstract 1Centro Universitario de Medicina Tropical (CUMETROP), Instituto de Investigaciones Biomédicas (IIBISMED), Facultad de Medicina, Universidad Mayor de San Simón, Cochabamba, Bolivia. 2Laboratorio de Radioinmunoensayo, Centro de Medicina Nuclear ahttps://orcid.org/0009-0006-3169-764X lilianverduguez@gmail.com bhttps://orcid.org/0000-0001-7896-9952 a.verduguez@umss.edu *Correspondencia: Aleida Verduguez Orellana Correo electrónico: a.verduguez@umss.edu Recibido el 30 de junio de 2026 Aceptado 16 de septiembre de 2026 https://doi.org/10.47993/gmb.v49i2.1344 L a severidad del Síndrome Cardiopulmonar por Hantavirus (HCPS), desde la perspectiva biológica, es causado por diferentes variantes de hantavirus, que circulan en la región de las américas; siendo la más severa la variante Andes (ANDV)1, 2. En cambio otras variantes tales como Laguna Negra (LNV), Río Mamoré (RIOMV), ocasionan un HCSP entre moderado y leve con mejor pronóstico de recuperación3,4. Desde la perspectiva clínica, el HCPS, como evento, inicia posterior a un período de incubación de unas 2 semanas en promedio4. La fase febril del HCPS inicia con síntomas inespecíficos como fiebre, cefalea, mialgias/artralgias, sintomatología gastrointestinal3,5 y ausencia de sintomatología del tracto respiratorio superior6, estos, aparecerán recién en la fase sindrómica. La fase cardiopulmonar inicia de manera súbita con disnea progresiva acompañada de tos, además de hipoxia severa, la cual se evidencia con cianosis peribucal y desaturación de pulso. Al tercer día el paciente presenta taquicardia e hipotensión3,7. La mitad de los afectados, desarrollan daño renal agudo y un tercio presenta shock. Es en esta fase donde ocurren la gran parte de los decesos3, 6. Los eventos inmunológicos implicados en el desencadenamiento del HCSP independientemente de la variante de hantavirus responsable de la infección, son complejos e interdependientes, con la participación de la inmunidad innata mediante las AR01 Artículos de Revisión Review Article 101 G MB julio-diciembre 2026 Gac Med Bol 2026; 49(2): células dendríticas y sus productos químicos próximas a las células endoteliales pulmonares, así como también la activación de la inmunidad adaptativa celular, principalmente de linfocitos CD8, complementadas con una desregulación de la respuesta inmune global caracterizada por una tormenta de citocinas4. El objetivo de la presente revisión es analizar los mecanismos inmunológicos que conducen al desarrollo del HCSP por la infección con las variantes de Hantavirus ANDV; RIOMV y LNV que circulan en el territorio boliviano y explicar desde esa perspectiva las manifestaciones clínicas que evidencian la presencia de este síndrome. Metodología Esta revisión sistemática se estructuró siguiendo los lineamientos de la declaración PRISMA 2020 y fue registrada en la plataforma internacional PROSPERO con el código CRD420261437203. Consultamos exhaustivamente las bases de datos PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase y Scopus para literatura publicada hasta junio de 2026. Para sistematizar la información, aplicamos una estrategia de búsqueda combinada mediante operadores booleanos (AND, OR) que integró términos MeSH, DeCS y palabras clave en texto libre: ("Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome"[Mesh] OR "Hantavirus"[Mesh] OR "Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome"[TiAb] OR "Andes virus"[TiAb] OR "Laguna Negra virus"[TiAb] OR "Rio Mamore virus"[TiAb]) AND ("Cytokine Storm"[Mesh] OR "Immunity, Innate"[Mesh] OR "Immunity, Cellular"[Mesh] OR "Capillary Permeability"[Mesh] OR "immunopathogenesis"[TiAb] OR "immune response"[TiAb] OR "Th1/Th17"[TiAb] OR "VEGF"[TiAb] OR "VE-cadherin"[TiAb]) AND ("South America"[Mesh] OR "Bolivia"[Mesh]). Se incluyo estudios observacionales, ensayos clínicos y modelos experimentales (in vitro e in vivo) enfocados en la inmunopatogenia de estas variantes sudamericanas y su relación con la gravedad clínica. analysis.background: HCPS caused by South American hantavirus variants is a severe, immune‑mediated disease, and understanding its immunopathology is needed for better management.
analysis.methods: A systematic review of the scientific literature was performed following PRISMA 2020 guidelines.
analysis.results: The Bolivian variants ANDV, RIOMV and LNV trigger HCPS; the virus infects endothelium without direct cytopathic damage; ANDV evades innate immunity accumulating high viral load, while RIOMV hyper‑stimulates macrophages with a Th1/Th17 profile; these pathways alter capillary permeability, producing non‑cardiogenic pulmonary edema and cardiogenic shock.
analysis.contribution: Identifying variant‑specific immune mechanisms provides insight for designing targeted anti‑inflammatory therapies, addressing the current lack of specific treatment.
analysis.limitations: No limitations are reported in the supplied evidence; the article is a review and does not present new primary data.

analysis.summary_en: Background: HCPS caused by South American hantavirus variants is a severe, immune‑mediated disease, prompting analysis of its immunopathology. Methods: A systematic review was conducted according to PRISMA 2020. Results: Variants ANDV, RIOMV and LNV in Bolivia trigger HCPS; the virus infects endothelium without direct cytopathic damage; ANDV evades innate immunity with high viral load, RIOMV hyper‑stimulates macrophages with a Th1/Th17 profile, leading to altered capillary permeability, non‑cardiogenic pulmonary edema and cardiogenic shock. Contribution: Clarifying these mechanisms highlights targets for anti‑inflammatory therapies, important because no specific treatment exists. Limitations: No limitations are reported in the supplied evidence; the work is a review, not new primary data.

papers.title: Epigenetics of HFRS: Linking Immunity, Pathogenesis, and Vaccine-Induced Protection.
papers.abstract: Haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), caused by Old World hantaviruses, including Hantaan virus (HTNV) and Seoul virus (SEOV), is an important public-health concern, particularly in Asia. Clinical manifestations range from febrile illness to vascular leakage, thrombocytopenia, haemorrhage and acute kidney injury. The mechanisms underlying variation in disease severity and the variability and durability of vaccine-induced immunity remain incompletely understood. Epigenetic mechanisms, including DNA methylation, histone modifications, chromatin regulation and non-coding RNA-mediated regulation, can influence antiviral immunity and immune-cell function in several biological settings; however, their specific contributions to HFRS remain insufficiently characterized. This structured narrative review examines hantavirus-specific evidence alongside relevant findings from other viral infections and vaccination settings, focusing on inflammatory responses, endothelial dysfunction, regulatory non-coding RNAs, trained immunity and potential applications in vaccinology. Experimental HTNV studies and clinical investigations of regulatory RNAs have identified candidate pathways associated with hantavirus-host interactions; however, these findings do not establish that epigenetic mechanisms determine HFRS severity or clinical outcomes. Similarly, preclinical hantavirus vaccine studies and early clinical evaluations provide evidence regarding immunogenicity and safety but do not demonstrate epigenetic mediation of protective immunity. Findings from Andes virus (ANDV), associated primarily with hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), and other viral systems are therefore considered comparative or contextual evidence, not directly generalizable to HFRS. This review identifies critical knowledge gaps and outlines how longitudinal, cell-resolved epigenomic profiling, functional validation and integrated multi-omics could clarify causal mechanisms, explain interindividual variation in disease outcomes and vaccine responses, and establish the potential translational value of epigenetic biomarkers and interventions.

Experimental HTNV studies and clinical investigations of regulatory RNAs have identified candidate pathways associated with hantavirus-host interactions; however, these findings do not establish that epigenetic mechanisms determine HFRS severity or clinical outcomes. Similarly, preclinical hantavirus vaccine studies and early clinical evaluations provide evidence regarding immunogenicity and safety but do not demonstrate epigenetic mediation of protective immunity. Findings from Andes virus (ANDV), associated primarily with hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), and other viral systems are therefore considered comparative or contextual evidence, not directly generalizable to HFRS. This review identifies critical knowledge gaps and outlines how longitudinal, cell-resolved epigenomic profiling, functional validation and integrated multi-omics could clarify causal mechanisms, explain interindividual variation in disease outcomes and vaccine responses, and establish the potential translational value of epigenetic biomarkers and interventions.

papers.title: Hantavirus RNA Detection in Small Mammals and Spatial Comparison with Reported Human HFRS Cases in West Kazakhstan Region, 2025
papers.abstract: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a zoonotic disease associated with orthohantaviruses maintained in natural rodent hosts. This study assessed the detection and spatial distribution of hantavirus RNA among small mammals in the West Kazakhstan Region in 2025 and compared rodent surveillance findings with human HFRS occurrence. An observational cross-sectional analytical study was conducted in July and September 2025 in four districts. A total of 343 small mammals were captured and morphologically identified. Lung tissue samples from 329 animals collected in September were examined in 123 pooled testing units, whereas 14 animals collected in July were tested individually. Thus, 137 testing units representing 343 animals were evaluated by real-time and conventional RT-PCR. The minimum infection rate (MIR) was calculated as a descriptive minimum estimate, and a pooled-testing likelihood model was used to account for variation in testing-unit size. Hantavirus RNA was detected in 47/137 testing units, including 45 positive pooled units and two individually positive specimens. Based on 343 individual animals, the descriptive MIR was 13.7%. The model-based individual-level infection probability was estimated at 18.0% (95% profile-likelihood CI: 13.5–23.1%). Positive testing units were observed among the Ural field mouse (Apodemus uralensis), bank vole (Myodes glareolus), and common vole (Microtus arvalis). At the district level, the descriptive MIR ranged from 11.6% in Burlinsky to 19.0% in Chingirlauisky. Sampling sites overlapped spatially with settlements reporting human HFRS cases, including Utvinka, Daryinsk, and Rubezhinskoye; however, spatial coincidence does not establish direct transmission.

papers.title_zh: 汉坦病毒 2025年哈萨克斯坦西部地区小型哺乳动物RNA检测及与报告的人类肾综合征出血热病例的空间比较

analysis_zh.background: 肾综合征出血热(HFRS)是一种人畜共患疾病,与在自然啮齿动物宿主中维持的正汉坦病毒相关。
analysis_zh.methods: 2025年7月和9月在哈萨克斯坦西部地区四个区开展了一项观察性横断面分析研究;捕获了343只小型哺乳动物,进行形态鉴定,并对329只动物的肺组织在123个合并检测单元和14个单独检测中进行检测,使用实时和常规RT‐PCR评估汉坦病毒 RNA。
analysis_zh.contribution: 该研究绘制了小型哺乳动物中汉坦病毒的流行分布图,并显示其与人类肾综合征出血热病例的空间重叠,突显了监测和公共卫生干预的潜在风险区域。
analysis_zh.limitations: 空间重合并不证明直接传播,且本研究仅限于摘要报告。

papers.title: Structural basis for protocadherin-1 recognition by New World hantaviruses.
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses are rodent-borne pathogens that cause severe human disease for which no approved therapeutics are available. New World hantaviruses, including Andes virus (ANDV), use the cell-surface receptor protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) to enter host cells1. However, the structural basis of this interaction remains unclear. Here we describe the structure of PCDH1 bound to the ANDV spike at near-atomic resolution. PCDH1 asymmetrically engages a deep central pocket formed by four Gn protomers in the spike, explaining why only intact viral particles or soluble tetramers recognize it. Mutagenesis identified three Gn loops that shape the receptor-binding site and afford the transfer of PCDH1 binding from New World to Old World glycoproteins. Structural and functional analyses of four neutralizing antibodies revealed that they block receptor binding through two distinct mechanisms—occluding access to the PCDH1-binding site or sterically preventing receptor engagement. Together, these findings define the structural determinants of hantavirus–receptor recognition, reveal how a virus can mask its receptor-binding site by recessing it in a surface depression and how antibodies can counter this strategy, and provide a framework for the design of antiviral therapeutics targeting the hantavirus spike. The structure of PCDH1 bound to the ANDV spike defines the structural determinants of hantavirus–receptor recognition.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses are rodent‑borne pathogens causing severe human disease with no approved therapeutics. Contribution: These findings define structural determinants of hantavirus‑receptor recognition, reveal viral masking of the binding site, and provide a framework for antiviral therapeutic design. papers.title: Risk Communication in a Post-Pandemic World: Lessons from the 2026 Andes Virus Outbreak
papers.abstract: In May 2026, a hantavirus outbreak aboard the MV Hondius cruise ship triggered public alarm disproportionate to its actual scale, despite the rapid diagnosis, clear WHO and ECDC guidance, and swift containment within three months. This commentary asks why outbreaks that health authorities handle correctly can still produce pandemic-level panic. Drawing on media framing research and the Hondius case itself, there seem to be two forces at work. One is news coverage that foregrounds alarming questions while burying expert reassurances. The second one is that post-pandemic public has learnt to distrust reassurance after Covid, when authorities failed to convey that guidance would evolve. This piece contends that clear, accurate and timely statements from health authorities are no longer sufficient on their own and proposes three practices going forward. Recommendations involve naming and directly addressing alarming narratives early, treating community trust as infrastructure built before a crisis rather than during one, and engaging with social media conversations directly rather than relying solely on content removal. Since it was small and well controlled, this outbreak offers a low-cost opportunity to test these practices before a larger outbreak makes the same communication gap far more costly.

analysis.background: The 2026 Andes (hantavirus) outbreak on the MV Hondius cruise ship sparked public alarm far beyond its actual scale despite rapid diagnosis, clear WHO/ECDC guidance, and swift containment.
analysis.main_directions: The commentary highlights two drivers of panic: sensationalist media framing that foregrounds alarming questions and a post‑COVID public distrust of official reassurance.
analysis.current_state: Media coverage tends to emphasize alarming narratives while burying expert reassurances, and the public now doubts evolving guidance from authorities.
analysis.gaps: Current risk communication—clear, accurate, timely statements—alone no longer prevents panic in the post‑pandemic environment.
analysis.future_research: The author proposes testing three practices—early naming of alarming narratives, building community trust before crises, and direct engagement with social‑media conversations—in future outbreaks.

analysis.summary_en: Background: The 2026 Andes virus outbreak on MV Hondius caused disproportionate alarm despite rapid containment. Main directions: Panic is driven by sensationalist media framing and post‑COVID distrust of reassurance. Current state: Media foregrounds alarming questions while expert reassurances are buried, and the public mistrusts evolving guidance. Gaps: Clear, timely statements from authorities are insufficient to prevent panic. Future research: Test early naming of alarming narratives, pre‑crisis trust building, and direct social‑media engagement in future events.

papers.title_zh: 后疫情时代的风险沟通:2026年安第斯病毒疫情的经验教训

analysis_zh.background: 2026年安第斯(汉坦病毒)在MV Hondius邮轮上的爆发,尽管诊断迅速、WHO/ECDC指南明确、控制措施迅速,却因公众恐慌远超实际规模。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 评论指出恐慌的两大驱动因素:渲染性媒体框架突出惊恐问题,以及后COVID时代公众对官方安抚的信任缺失。
analysis_zh.current_state: 媒体报道倾向于强调惊恐叙事而埋没专家安抚,公众如今对当局不断变化的指导持怀疑态度。
analysis_zh.gaps: 在后疫情环境中,仅靠清晰、准确、及时的风险沟通——即明确的声明——已不足以防止恐慌。
analysis_zh.future_research: 作者建议在未来疫情中测试三项做法:提前命名惊恐叙事、在危机前建立社区信任、以及直接参与社交媒体对话。

papers.title: Hantaviruses as Emerging Zoonotic Pathogens: Molecular Biology, Epidemiology, Therapeutics, vaccine, and Pathogenesis.
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses are globally distributed zoonotic pathogens belonging to the family Hantaviridae and are responsible for two major human diseases, hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS). Despite substantial progress in hantavirus research, important challenges remain in understanding the interactions among viral evolution, reservoir ecology, environmental change, transmission dynamics, and host immunopathology. This review provides an integrated One Health perspective that connects molecular virology and host-virus interactions with transmission ecology, global epidemiology, and the mechanisms underlying vascular leakage and severe disease. In addition to summarizing established knowledge, we highlight recent advances in hantavirus taxonomy, genomic and molecular surveillance, ecological and transmission modeling, and the identification of hantavirus circulation in previously underrecognized regions. Particular emphasis is placed on the role of reservoir host dynamics, climate and environmental change, habitat disturbance, and human-wildlife interactions in shaping spillover risk, as well as on endothelial dysfunction, immune dysregulation, and coagulation abnormalities as interconnected mechanisms of disease severity. We also identify persistent knowledge gaps concerning host susceptibility, viral persistence, determinants of differential virulence and tissue tropism, interspecies transmission, and the development of effective antiviral therapies and vaccines. By integrating these complementary perspectives, this review provides a framework for understanding hantavirus emergence and pathogenesis while identifying priorities for future surveillance, prevention, and therapeutic research.

In addition to summarizing established knowledge, we highlight recent advances in hantavirus taxonomy, genomic and molecular surveillance, ecological and transmission modeling, and the identification of hantavirus circulation in previously underrecognized regions. Particular emphasis is placed on the role of reservoir host dynamics, climate and environmental change, habitat disturbance, and human-wildlife interactions in shaping spillover risk, as well as on endothelial dysfunction, immune dysregulation, and coagulation abnormalities as interconnected mechanisms of disease severity. By integrating these complementary perspectives, this review provides a framework for understanding hantavirus emergence and pathogenesis while identifying priorities for future surveillance, prevention, and therapeutic research.

papers.title: Expanded protocadherin-1 usage reveals a broader hantavirus entry landscape.
papers.abstract: Mammalian hantaviruses are RNA viruses that cause hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome in the Americas and hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in Eurasia. The cellular entry mechanisms of most hantaviruses remain poorly defined. To examine entry by phylogenetically distinct hantaviruses identified across Africa, Eurasia, and the Americas, we generated replication-competent recombinant vesicular stomatitis viruses (rVSVs) bearing Gn/Gc proteins from Necoclí, Sangassou, Thottapalayam, Kenkeme, Nova, Oxbow, and Tula viruses. All these Gn/Gc proteins except Kenkeme supported infection of primary human endothelial cells, indicating that endothelial cell entry is permissive for a broader range of hantaviruses than previously appreciated. Except for rVSV-Kenkeme, these rVSVs did not acquire additional mutations beyond pre-engineered rescue-enhancing changes during rescue and passaging. Genetic studies in human cells lacking protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) showed that Necoclí, Tula, and Nova viruses use PCDH1 for efficient infection, although the Nova phenotype was weaker. These three Gn/Gc proteins bound soluble PCDH1 with different apparent avidities, and infection by the corresponding rVSVs was inhibited by soluble PCDH1; Necoclí and Tula, but not Nova, were also blocked by a PCDH1-targeting monoclonal antibody. Authentic Tula virus infection was similarly reduced in PCDH1 knockout endothelial cells. Finally, the broadly reactive anti-Gn/Gc human monoclonal antibody ADI-42898 efficiently neutralized Necoclí, Nova, Sangassou, and Kenkeme rVSVs, but showed weak or undetectable activity against Oxbow, Tula, and Thottapalayam rVSVs. Together, these findings expand the range of hantavirus glycoproteins capable of mediating infection of human endothelial cells, broaden the phylogenetic scope of PCDH1-dependent entry, and identify receptor-targeted and viral glycoprotein-targeted strategies with differential activity.IMPORTANCEMany newly discovered hantaviruses are known only from sequence data, leaving their ability to enter human cells and their receptor usage unresolved. Using a BSL2-compatible recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus (rVSV) system, we show that glycoproteins from several divergent hantaviruses can mediate infection of primary human endothelial cells, indicating that endothelial cell entry is permissive for a broader range of hantaviruses than previously appreciated. We also show that protocadherin-1 (PCDH1), previously linked mainly to New World hantaviruses, is used by Necoclí, Tula, and Nova viruses but not universally across the panel, revealing broader but heterogeneous receptor usage. An authentic Tula virus experiment supports this conclusion beyond the surrogate system. Finally, a broadly reactive anti-Gn/Gc antibody neutralizes several, but not all, of these viruses, highlighting both the promise and the limits of broadly protective countermeasures and the utility of these rVSVs for evaluating entry inhibitors.
