We 52 also show that protocadherin-1 (PCDH1), previously linked mainly to New World 53 hantaviruses, is used by Necoclí, Tula, and Nova viruses but not universally across the 54 panel, revealing broader but heterogeneous receptor usage. An authentic Tula virus 55 experiment supports this conclusion beyond the surrogate system. Finally, a broadly 56 reactive anti-Gn/Gc antibody neutralizes several, but not all, of these viruses, highlighting 57 both the promise and the limits of broadly protective countermeasures and the utility of 58 these rVSVs for evaluating entry inhibitors. 59 60 Page 4 of 40 Introduction 61 Hantaviruses are enveloped, negative-sense RNA viruses that belong to the family 62 Hantaviridae in the order Elliovirales(1). When humans are accidentally exposed to 63 aerosolized excreta from infected reservoir hosts, rodent-borne hantaviruses can cause 64 severe, often fatal diseases, such as hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) in 65 the Americas and hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in Europe and Asia(2, 66 3). Periodic hantavirus outbreaks continue to occur, and Andes virus (ANDV) is notable 67 for rare human-to-human transmission in a close-contact setting, such as on the MV 68 Hondius Cruise Ship in April-May 2026(4–7). Despite their significant impact on public 69 health, there are currently no FDA-approved vaccines or therapeutics for hantavirus 70 infections, and our understanding of their entry mechanisms remains poor(2, 8). 71 Studies based on genetic sequencing over the past few decades have discovered 72 many new mammalian hantaviruses carried by rodents, insectivores, and bats(9, 10). 73 Currently, the International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses (ICTV) recognizes 48 74 species of mammalian hantaviruses globally(11). However, for most of these 75 hantaviruses, no virus isolates are available, and their potential to cause human infection 76 and illness remains unknown(12). Additionally, the need for high-level biocontainment 77 (BSL3) in hantavirus research and the lack of a robust reverse genetics systems to study 78 the complete hantavirus infection cycle greatly hinder our understanding of their 79 biology(2). 80 Hantavirus particles carry a negative-sense, tripartite genome composed of small 81 (S), medium (M), and large (L) segments(13). The S segment encodes the nucleoprotein 82 (N), which coats the genome; the L segment encodes the L protein, which possesses 83 Page 5 of 40 RNA-dependent RNA polymerase and endoribonuclease activities required for genome 84 replication and transcription, respectively. The M segment encodes the glycoprotein 85 complex as a single polyprotein, which is processed by cellular proteases to generate the 86 Gn and Gc glycoproteins(14). The Gn/Gc heterodimers are arranged in a tetrameric 87 cloverleaf-like structure on hantavirus particles, forming spikes(15). Gn is believed to 88 interact with host receptors, while Gc mediates fusion of the viral and endosomal 89 membranes during cellular entry(2, 15). Because Gn/Gc are necessary and sufficient to 90 mediate cellular entry, vesicular stomatitis viruses carrying Gn/Gc serve as powerful tools 91 for studying viral entry(2, 16). 92 Among proposed hantavirus entry receptors, only protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) has 93 compelling in vivo support; it is required for infection and pathogenesis of ANDV in Syrian 94 hamsters(17, 18). Earlier in vitro studies have implicated β1-3 integrins (ITGβ1, ITGβ2, 95 ITGβ3), decay-accelerating factor (DAF)/CD55, and the globular head of C1q receptor 96 (gC1qR) as potential attachment factors or receptors for hantavirus entry(19–24). 97 However, their in vivo relevance is not clear, and ITGβ1, ITGβ3 and DAF/CD55 are not 98 essential for hantavirus infection in human endothelial cells, the major targets of 99 hantavirus infection(25). Genetic knockout and biochemical studies demonstrated that 100 protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) is required for the entry of 5 species of New World 101 hantaviruses: Andes virus, Sin Nombre virus (SNV), Prospect Hill virus, Maporal virus, 102 and Choclo virus, but not for the Old World hantaviruses such as Hantaan virus (HTNV), 103 Puumala virus, and Seoul virus(18, 25). The first extracellular cadherin (EC1) domain of 104 PCDH1 binds the Gn/Gc of New World hantaviruses, and disruption of the PCDH1:Gn/Gc 105 interaction by complete knockout or point mutations in EC1 protects Syrian hamsters 106 Page 6 of 40 against a lethal Andes virus challenge(17, 18). Moreover, soluble PCDH1 carrying the 107 EC1 domain and the EC1-specific monoclonal antibody (mAb-3305) neutralize rVSV- 108 ANDV and SNV infections(17, 18). However, the extent of PCDH1 usage by distinct 109 hantavirus lineages remains unknown. 110 To capture genetic, geographic, and reservoir-host variation, we focused on shrew- 111 borne Thottapalayam virus (TPMV) and Kenkeme virus (KKMV); mole-borne Nova virus 112 (NVAV), and Oxbow virus (OXBV); New World rodent-borne Necoclí virus (NECV); Old 113 World rodent-borne Sangassou virus (SANGV), and vole-borne Tula virus (TULV)(26). 114 Thottapalayam virus was first isolated from the Asian house shrew in India(27), and 115 Kenkeme virus was identified in the flat-skulled shrew in Russia(28). Nova virus is a highly 116 divergent mole-borne virus of the European mole and was initially detected in Hungary, 117 with high prevalence later documented in France(29, 30). Necoclí virus is principally 118 associated with Cherrie’s cane rat in Colombia(31). Sangassou virus is the first 119 indigenous African hantavirus isolate and was identified in the African wood mouse in 120 Guinea(32). Tula virus is classically associated with common voles and related arvicoline 121 hosts across Eurasia(26, 33). Among these viruses, Sangassou virus entry studies 122 implicated integrin β1 as a receptor(32), whereas Tula virus has the strongest direct 123 evidence of human relevance, with a molecularly confirmed symptomatic infection 124 reported in an immunocompetent patient(34). While serologic evidence suggests possible 125 human exposure to Thottapalayam and Sangassou viruses, the ability of Kenkeme, Nova, 126 Oxbow, and Necoclí viruses to cause human infection or disease remains unknown(35– 127 38). Although their reservoir-host associations are better established, human-cell tropism 128 and receptor usage remain poorly characterized for most of these viruses(26, 38). 129 Page 7 of 40 Together, these phylogenetically divergent hantaviruses associated with a variety of 130 reservoir hosts provide a framework to evaluate human cell-tropism and PCDH1 131 dependence across mammalian hantaviruses. 132 Here, we generated rVSVs expressing the Gn/Gc proteins of the seven genetically 133 and ecologically heterogeneous hantaviruses mentioned above to investigate their entry 134 mechanisms and host receptor usage. Infectivity assays in human cells, including primary 135 endothelial cells, demonstrated that these Gn/Gc, except that of Kenkeme virus, can 136 mediate infection of human cells without acquiring additional adaptive mutations. 137 Experiments with PCDH1 knockout human cells and ELISA-based binding assays 138 demonstrated that Necoclí, Tula, and Nova virus Gn/Gc-mediated infections depend on 139 PCDH1. Finally, we demonstrated the utility of PCDH1 and Gn/Gc-targeting approaches 140 for neutralizing these viral infections. 141 Results 142 Divergent hantavirus Gn/Gc proteins mediate infection of human endothelial cells 143 Hantavirus Gn/Gc sequences are highly divergent across species, with 40-60% amino 144 acid differences between them. Our hantavirus panel was selected to sample viruses 145 spanning diverse reservoir hosts, phylogenetic lineages and geographic origins (Fig. 1). 146 To enable cellular entry studies of these hantaviruses at BSL2, we generated 147 recombinant vesicular stomatitis viruses (rVSVs) expressing Gn/Gc in place of the native 148 VSV G protein. These viruses also express an enhanced GFP reporter (Fig. 2A, top 149 panel). 150 Because New World hantavirus glycoproteins are more compatible with plasma- 151 membrane budding, whereas Old World hantavirus glycoproteins are typically Golgi- 152 Page 8 of 40 localized, rVSVs bearing New World hantavirus Gn/Gc are generally rescued without 153 adaptive mutations(39, 40). In contrast, Old World hantaviruses, such as Hantaan virus 154 and Dobrava-Belgrade virus, require two mutations, I532K in the cytoplasmic tail of Gn, 155 and S1094L in the membrane-proximal part of the Gc ectodomain, to enhance rVSV 156 generation(16). These mutations are unlikely to directly affect receptor engagement 157 because they were previously shown to enhance rVSV infectivity primarily by altering 158 glycoprotein localization and incorporation into virions(16). Accordingly, we preemptively 159 altered the Gn/Gc sequences of Thottapalayam, Kenkeme, Nova, Oxbow, and 160 Sangassou viruses to incorporate HTNV-adaptive changes for rVSV generation (Fig. 2A, 161 bottom panel). 162 Plasmids encoding cognate rVSV genomes carrying codon-optimized Gn/Gc sequences 163 for expression in human cells were transfected into 293FT cells together with the helper 164 plasmids, and the resulting supernatants were used to infect Huh7.51 cells for viral 165 amplification and stock generation. These viruses reached titers of 5-6 log10 per mL in 166 Huh7.5.1 cells. Sequencing of the Gn/Gc inserts in the rVSV genomes confirmed that 167 none of the rVSVs, except rVSV-Kenkeme, acquired additional mutations beyond the pre- 168 engineered ones. In rVSV-Kenkeme, a G485R mutation, numbered according to the 169 glycoprotein precursor, was detected, although its significance remains unclear. 170 To compare infectivity, we normalized viral input by titrating the rVSVs on permissive 171 Huh7.5.1 cells. These titers were then used to determine the multiplicity of infection (MOI) 172 for infection of primary human pulmonary microvascular endothelial cells (HPMECs), a 173 major target cell type for hantavirus infection. HPMECs were infected at an MOI of 1 and 174 fixed 24 hours later to assess eGFP-positive cells. All rVSVs except rVSV-Kenkeme 175 Page 9 of 40 infected these cells, although with varying efficiency (Fig. 2B). For quantitative analysis, 176 we evaluated infection at MOIs of 0.2, 1, and 5 at 8 hours post-infection. At an MOI of 177 0.2, only rVSV-Tula infection was evident (4.68%). At MOIs of 1 and 5, rVSV-Tula (23% 178 and 38%, respectively) and rVSV-Thottapalayam (6% and 18%, respectively) infection 179 was detectable, along with the positive controls rVSV-ANDV and rVSV-HTNV, whereas 180 the remaining viruses were not (Fig. 2C, left panel). 181 Kinetic experiments over 48 hrs at MOIs of 0.2 and 1 (Fig. 2C, middle and right panels, 182 respectively) further supported the higher infectivity of rVSV-Thottapalayam and rVSV- 183 Tula, and also revealed substantial infection by rVSV-Necoclí (18 and 36% at 12 hours, 184 respectively) and rVSV-Nova (32 and 38% at 48 hours, respectively). The other three 185 rVSVs, rVSV-Sangassou, rVSV-Oxbow, and rVSV-Kenkeme, showed much lower 186 infectivity: rVSV-Sangassou peaked at 11%, rVSV-Oxbow at 5%, and rVSV-Kenkeme 187 remained barely detectable (<2%). Three broad kinetic patterns were observed: rVSV- 188 Thottapalayam, rVSV-Nova, and, to a lesser extent, rVSV-Sangassou showed a steady 189 increase over time, similar to rVSV-ANDV and rVSV-HTNV; rVSV-Necoclí and rVSV-Tula 190 showed relatively higher infection with little increase over time; and rVSV-Kekeme and 191 rVSV-Oxbow showed very low infection with no increase over time (Fig. 2C). Except Kenkeme virus, this activity was 194 retained without acquisition of additional mutations beyond the pre-engineered changes 195 during rVSV generation. 196 PCDH1 knockout reduces infection by rVSVs bearing Necoclí, Tula, and Nova virus 197 Gn/Gc-mediated entry 198 Page 10 of 40 We have previously used PCDH1 knockout human osteosarcoma U2OS cells to evaluate 199 PCDH1's role in hantavirus infection(17, 18). To assess PCDH1 usage by these rVSVs, 200 we infected WT U2OS cells, a clonal PCDH1 knockout (KO) U2OS cell line, and PCDH1 201 KO U2OS cells complemented with PCDH1 cDNA with pre-titrated amounts of rVSVs 202 selected to yield 20-30% infection in WT cells, except for rVSV-Kenkeme, for which the 203 target infection level was 10%, and quantified infection 24 hours later (Fig. 3A). Although rVSV-Necoclí and rVSV-Nova infection 206 was also reduced in PCDH1 KO cells, it was not restored in the complemented U2OS 207 cells. Infection by the other 4 rVSVs was unaffected by PCDH1 status. 208 To verify these results in endothelial cells, we tested the same rVSV infections in human 209 TIME endothelial cells, as in our previous work(25). The results in TIME cells were largely 210 consistent with those in U2OS cells: rVSV-ANDV infection decreased by about 80%; 211 rVSV-Necoclí and rVSV-Tula infection each decreased by about 80%; and rVSV-Nova 212 infection decreased by about 50% in the absence of PCDH1 (Fig. 3B). Importantly, 213 infection of all 4 viruses was restored by PCDH1 complementation in this nonclonal 214 knockout population. In contrast, rVSV-Oxbow, rVSV-Kenkeme, rVSV-Thottapalayam, 215 and rVSV-Sangassou infections were unaffected by PCDH1. These results demonstrate 216 that PCDH1 ablation in human cells reduces infection mediated by Necoclí, Tula, and 217 Nova Gn/Gc. 218 Necoclí, Tula, and Nova Gn/Gc specifically bind to PCDH1 219 To determine whether these Gn/Gc bind PCDH1, we first normalized input rVSVs by 220 measuring the VSV matrix (M) protein by Western blotting (Fig. 3A, top panel). We then 221 Page 11 of 40 used our previously validated ELISA, in which rVSV particles bearing hantavirus Gn/Gc 222 are captured by the soluble EC1-2 (sEC1-2) domain of PCDH1 immobilized on an ELISA 223 plate (17, 18). As with rVSV-ANDV, binding of rVSV-Necoclí to PCDH1 was dose 224 dependent, although of lower avidity (Fig. 4A, bottom panel). Binding of rVSV-Tula and 225 rVSV-Nova was weaker and was detectable only at higher virion inputs (Fig. 4B). 226 We next tested whether the EC1-specific mAb-3305 could block this interaction. 227 Preincubation of sEC1-2-coated plates with mAb-3305 before addition of rVSVs caused 228 a dose-dependent…

full_text_sections.full_text: Page 1 of 40 Expanded protocadherin-1 usage reveals a broader hantavirus entry landscape 1 2 Cierra Word1, Nahomi Guerra-Pilaquinga1, Ezgi Kasikci2, Lohit Khera1,†, Ramandeep 3 Kaur1, Upendra P. Lambe1, Maria Eugenia Dieterle2,‡, Kartik Chandran2, Rohit K. Jangra1,* 4 5 1 Department of Microbiology and Immunology, Center for Applied Immunology and 6 Pathological Processes, Center for Cardiovascular Diseases and Sciences, Louisiana 7 State University Health Sciences Center-Shreveport, Shreveport, Louisiana, USA. 8 2 Department of Microbiology and Immunology, Albert Einstein College of Medicine, 9 Bronx, New York, USA. 10 11 † Current address: Norgen Biotek, Thorold, Ontario, Canada. 12 ‡ Current address: Fundacion Instituto Leloir, Buenos Aires, Argentina. 13 14 * Corresponding author: Rohit K Jangra (rohit.jangra@lsuhs.edu) 15 16 17 Word counts: 18 19 Abstract: 243 20 Importance: 139 21 Text word count: 6367 22 Page 2 of 40 Abstract 23 Mammalian hantaviruses are RNA viruses that cause hantavirus cardiopulmonary 24 syndrome in the Americas and hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in Eurasia. The 25 cellular entry mechanisms of most hantaviruses remain poorly defined. To examine entry 26 by phylogenetically distinct hantaviruses, we generated replication-competent 27 recombinant vesicular stomatitis viruses (rVSVs) bearing Gn/Gc proteins from Necoclí, 28 Sangassou, Thottapalayam, Kenkeme, Nova, Oxbow, and Tula viruses. All these Gn/Gc 29 proteins except Kenkeme supported infection of primary human endothelial cells, 30 indicating that endothelial cell entry is permissive for a broader range of hantaviruses than 31 previously appreciated. Except for rVSV-Kenkeme, these rVSVs did not acquire additional 32 mutations beyond pre-engineered rescue-enhancing changes during rescue and 33 passaging. Genetic studies in human cells lacking protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) showed that 34 Necoclí, Tula, and Nova viruses use PCDH1 for efficient infection, although the Nova 35 phenotype was weaker. These three Gn/Gc proteins bound soluble PCDH1 with different 36 apparent avidities, and infection by the corresponding rVSVs was inhibited by soluble 37 PCDH1; Necoclí and Tula, but not Nova, were also blocked by a PCDH1-targeting 38 monoclonal antibody. Authentic Tula virus infection was similarly reduced in PCDH1 39 knockout endothelial cells. Finally, the broadly reactive anti-Gn/Gc human monoclonal 40 antibody ADI-42898 efficiently neutralized Necoclí, Nova, Sangassou, and Kenkeme 41 rVSVs but showed weak or undetectable activity against Oxbow, Tula, and Thottapalayam 42 rVSVs. Together, these findings expand the range of hantavirus glycoproteins capable of 43 mediating infection of human endothelial cells, broaden the phylogenetic scope of 44 Page 3 of 40 PCDH1-dependent entry, and identify receptor-targeted and viral glycoprotein-targeted 45 strategies with differential activity. 46 Importance 47 Many newly discovered hantaviruses are known only from sequence data, leaving their 48 ability to enter human cells and their receptor usage unresolved. Using a BSL2- 49 compatible rVSV system, we show that glycoproteins from several divergent hantaviruses 50 can mediate infection of primary human endothelial cells, indicating that endothelial cell 51 entry is permissive for a broader range of hantaviruses than previously appreciated. We 52 also show that protocadherin-1 (PCDH1), previously linked mainly to New World 53 hantaviruses, is used by Necoclí, Tula, and Nova viruses but not universally across the 54 panel, revealing broader but heterogeneous receptor usage. An authentic Tula virus 55 experiment supports this conclusion beyond the surrogate system. Finally, a broadly 56 reactive anti-Gn/Gc antibody neutralizes several, but not all, of these viruses, highlighting 57 both the promise and the limits of broadly protective countermeasures and the utility of 58 these rVSVs for evaluating entry inhibitors. 59 60 Page 4 of 40 Introduction 61 Hantaviruses are enveloped, negative-sense RNA viruses that belong to the family 62 Hantaviridae in the order Elliovirales(1). When humans are accidentally exposed to 63 aerosolized excreta from infected reservoir hosts, rodent-borne hantaviruses can cause 64 severe, often fatal diseases, such as hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) in 65 the Americas and hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in Europe and Asia(2, 66 3). Periodic hantavirus outbreaks continue to occur, and Andes virus (ANDV) is notable 67 for rare human-to-human transmission in a close-contact setting, such as on the MV 68 Hondius Cruise Ship in April-May 2026(4–7). Despite their significant impact on public 69 health, there are currently no FDA-approved vaccines or therapeutics for hantavirus 70 infections, and our understanding of their entry mechanisms remains poor(2, 8). 71 Studies based on genetic sequencing over the past few decades have discovered 72 many new mammalian hantaviruses carried by rodents, insectivores, and bats(9, 10). 73 Currently, the International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses (ICTV) recognizes 48 74 species of mammalian hantaviruses globally(11). However, for most of these 75 hantaviruses, no virus isolates are available, and their potential to cause human infection 76 and illness remains unknown(12). Additionally, the need for high-level biocontainment 77 (BSL3) in hantavirus research and the lack of a robust reverse genetics systems to study 78 the complete hantavirus infection cycle greatly hinder our understanding of their 79 biology(2). 80 Hantavirus particles carry a negative-sense, tripartite genome composed of small 81 (S), medium (M), and large (L) segments(13). The S segment encodes the nucleoprotein 82 (N), which coats the genome; the L segment encodes the L protein, which possesses 83 Page 5 of 40 RNA-dependent RNA polymerase and endoribonuclease activities required for genome 84 replication and transcription, respectively. The M segment encodes the glycoprotein 85 complex as a single polyprotein, which is processed by cellular proteases to generate the 86 Gn and Gc glycoproteins(14). The Gn/Gc heterodimers are arranged in a tetrameric 87 cloverleaf-like structure on hantavirus particles, forming spikes(15). Gn is believed to 88 interact with host receptors, while Gc mediates fusion of the viral and endosomal 89 membranes during cellular entry(2, 15). Because Gn/Gc are necessary and sufficient to 90 mediate cellular entry, vesicular stomatitis viruses carrying Gn/Gc serve as powerful tools 91 for studying viral entry(2, 16). 92 Among proposed hantavirus entry receptors, only protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) has 93 compelling in vivo support; it is required for infection and pathogenesis of ANDV in Syrian 94 hamsters(17, 18). Earlier in vitro studies have implicated β1-3 integrins (ITGβ1, ITGβ2, 95 ITGβ3), decay-accelerating factor (DAF)/CD55, and the globular head of C1q receptor 96 (gC1qR) as potential attachment factors or receptors for hantavirus entry(19–24). 97 However, their in vivo relevance is not clear, and ITGβ1, ITGβ3 and DAF/CD55 are not 98 essential for hantavirus infection in human endothelial cells, the major targets of 99 hantavirus infection(25). Genetic knockout and biochemical studies demonstrated that 100 protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) is required for the entry of 5 species of New World 101 hantaviruses: Andes virus, Sin Nombre virus (SNV), Prospect Hill virus, Maporal virus, 102 and Choclo virus, but not for the Old World hantaviruses such as Hantaan virus (HTNV), 103 Puumala virus, and Seoul virus(18, 25). The first extracellular cadherin (EC1) domain of 104 PCDH1 binds the Gn/Gc of New World hantaviruses, and disruption of the PCDH1:Gn/Gc 105 interaction by complete knockout or point mutations in EC1 protects Syrian hamsters 106 Page 6 of 40 against a lethal Andes virus challenge(17, 18). Moreover, soluble PCDH1 carrying the 107 EC1 domain and the EC1-specific monoclonal antibody (mAb-3305) neutralize rVSV- 108 ANDV…

analysis.background: Mammalian hantaviruses cause severe diseases like HCPS and HFRS, yet their cellular entry mechanisms are poorly defined, and many newly discovered species lack virus isolates for study.
analysis.methods: The study generated replication-competent recombinant vesicular stomatitis viruses (rVSVs) bearing Gn/Gc proteins from seven phylogenetically distinct hantaviruses to test infection of primary human endothelial cells and receptor usage.
analysis.results: All rVSVs except Kenkeme supported endothelial cell infection; Necoclí, Tula, and Nova viruses used PCDH1 for entry, with authentic Tula virus confirming this in knockout cells; antibody ADI-42898 neutralized some but not all rVSVs.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Mammalian hantaviruses cause severe diseases, but their entry mechanisms are poorly defined, and many species lack isolates. Methods: Researchers generated replication-competent recombinant vesicular stomatitis viruses (rVSVs) bearing Gn/Gc proteins from seven distinct hantaviruses to assess entry into primary human endothelial cells. Results: All rVSVs except Kenkeme supported endothelial infection. Genetic studies showed Necoclí, Tula, and Nova viruses use protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) for entry, a finding confirmed for Tula virus in authentic infection. Antibody ADI-42898 neutralized some rVSVs but not others. Contribution: The study expands the known range of hantaviruses entering human endothelial cells, broadens the phylogenetic scope of PCDH1-dependent entry, and provides a BSL2-compatible system for testing entry inhibitors. Limitations: The evidence is limited to the abstract and partial text, lacking specific quantitative data on binding avidities or neutralization titers, and relies on surrogate rVSV systems for most viruses.

papers.title: An ONT sequencing framework for hantavirus genome assembly, variant analysis, and defective viral genome characterization from whole-segment amplicons
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Orthohantaviruses are zoonotic, tri-segmented negative-sense RNA viruses of rodents and other small mammals that can cause severe human disease. Whole genome sequencing remains difficult because of low viral loads, high sequence diversity, and an inherent instability of the viral L segment. Current tiled amplicon and hybrid-capture approaches do not capture the heterogeneity of virus populations, including defective viral genomes (DVGs), which have never been described for hantaviruses. Here, we present an Oxford Nanopore Technologies sequencing framework based on universal reverse transcription primers targeting the conserved genome termini of orthohantaviruses and a single species-specific primer pair per segment, enabling amplification and sequencing of complete S, M, and L segments. We also developed an accompanying bioinformatic pipeline that performs reference-guided assembly of hantavirus genomes, consensus generation, variant calling, and DVG classification using the newly developed ORCHID classification pipeline. We applied this approach to diverse Puumala virus strains from infected cell cultures and bank voles, to representative Old World and New World orthohantaviruses, and to highly pathogenic New World viruses in vivo. In all cases we were able to accurately reconstruct full hantavirus genomes. Notably, we found that hantavirus populations contain highly abundant DVGs and conserved L segment deletions, whereas the S and M segments remained largely intact. Together, this work provides a low-cost, broadly applicable and easily customisable workflow for hantavirus genomics and reveals DVGs as a previously unrecognized feature of hantavirus populations. IMPORTANCE Hantaviruses cause severe and often fatal human diseases, and their diversity and low viral loads make them hard to sequence, which limits surveillance and outbreak investigation. We describe a simple, universal but customisable, low-cost nanopore sequencing workflow that recovers complete genome segments, including the full-length L segment, from cell culture and animal tissues across the entire Orthohantavirus genus. Using this approach, we report the first evidence of defective viral genomes in hantaviruses. These truncated genomes arise mainly from the L segment, which encodes the viral polymerase, and are formed at conserved genomic regions. Defective viral genomes can modulate viral replication, innate immune activation, and persistence in other viruses. Their presence in hantaviruses raises new questions about polymerase function, tolerance in reservoir hosts, and immune-mediated disease in humans. Our framework offers a practical tool for hantavirus genomics and a foundation for investigating how defective genomes shape hantavirus infection.

Human infections occur primarily through 81 inhalation of aerosolized excreta from infected animal hosts and can cause severe 82 disease, including haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and nephropathia 83 epidemica (NE) caused by Old World hantaviruses primarily in Eurasia and hantavirus 84 cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) caused by New World hantaviruses in the Americas 85 (2, 3). Case fatality rates for hantavirus diseases vary significantly depending on the 86 infecting virus species (4): it ranges from <1% for Puumala virus (PUUV), the causative 87 agent for NE, to up to 15% for HFRS-causing Old World hantaviruses such as Hantaan 88 virus (HTNV) in East Asia and Dobrava-Belgrade virus (DOBV) in eastern Europe, and 89 over 30% for HCPS-causing New World hantaviruses such as Andes virus (ANDV) and 90 Sin Nombre virus (SNV). 91 Hantaviruses have small tripartite negative-sense RNA genomes comprising the small 92 (S), medium (M) and large (L) genome segments, encoding only 4-5 viral proteins (5). 93 The S segment encodes the nucleoprotein (NP) and in some cases a non-structural 94 (NS) protein, the M segment encodes the glycoprotein precursor (GPC) which is co- 95 translationally cleaved into the Gn and Gc glycoproteins, and the L segment encodes 96 the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp). The genetic sequence divergence at the 97 amino acid level is significant across the hantavirus family (up to 75%) and even within 98 a species (up to 24%) (6). Low viral RNA copy numbers in clinical and rodent samples, 99 and natural RNA degradation outside of infected hosts makes obtaining complete 100 coverage of hantavirus genomes challenging (7, 8). Current state-of-the-art sequencing 101 approaches include metagenome sequencing, tiled amplicon sequencing and hybrid 102 capture-based sequencing, which all require extensive optimisation and large numbers 103 of probes (9–12). Existing long-read amplicon-based sequencing approaches often 104 include single amplicons for the smaller segments, but to date, there are no established 105 protocols to reliably capture the entire L segment in a single amplicon. In addition, while 106 these methods can provide full genome coverage sequencing and provide consensus 107 sequences of viruses, they do not accurately reflect the genetic makeup of any given 108 virus population. In reality, virus populations are highly heterogeneous and contain large 109 proportions of defective viral genomes (DVGs) consisting of genome truncations, 110 duplications and recombinations (13). However, DVGs have so far never been reported 111 for hantaviruses. 112 Here, we designed a whole segment amplicon-based long-read nanopore sequencing 113 method and an end-to-end bioinformatical analysis pipeline for hantavirus genome 114 assembly, alignment, consensus sequence generation, variant calling and defective 115 viral genome analysis (Fig.1A). This approach minimises required optimisation steps for 116 tiling and hybridization probes and enables a much more accurate depiction of 117 heterogenous virus populations without sacrificing sensitivity or genome coverage. 118 Using this method, we were able to sequence several diverse PUUV strains from both 119 infected cell cultures and from bank voles – their natural host species. In addition, we 120 validated our method using representative members of the whole Orthohantavirus 121 genus and samples obtained from cell cultures and animal tissues. Our sequencing 122 4 approach provides a cost-effective and rapid end-to-end pipeline to analyse hantavirus 123 genomes from environmental, animal and cellular samples. In addition, we provide the 124 first report of hantavirus DVGs and provide a framework for their analysis. 125 126 127 RESULTS 128 A nanopore sequencing and bioinformatics pipeline. Here, we designed a 129 whole segment amplicon-based long-read nanopore sequencing method. Hantavirus 130 RNA is reverse transcribed using universal hantavirus primers that hybridize with the 131 highly conserved 14 nucleotides at the genome termini. Subsequently, each genome 132 segment is amplified in a virus species-specific manner using a single longer primer pair 133 corresponding to the specific genome termini of a virus genome segment. PCR 134 products are then sequenced using Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) long-read 135 sequencing technology. This is followed by a bioinformatical analysis pipeline that 136 includes hantavirus reference-guided genome assembly, genome alignment, consensus 137 sequence generation, variant calling and DVG analysis (Fig.1A). The DVG analysis is 138 performed using the ‘ONT-based Recombination and Copy-back Haplotype 139 Identification for DVGs’ (ORCHID) pipeline which detects recombination events in virus 140 genomes and classifies these as artefacts, deletion, or copy-back events (Fig. 1B). 141 Deletion DVGs (delVGs) are produced when the RdRp dissociates from the genome 142 template during replication, continues reading the template without copying any of it, 143 and then reassociates and starts copying the template further downstream, thus 144 creating an internal deletion of the copied genome (Fig. 1C). Copy-back DVGs (cbVGs) 145 are produced when the RdRp dissociates from the template strand during replication 146 and reengages the nascent product strand as a new template (Fig. 1C). Together, this 147 workflow represents a highly customisable end-to-end sequencing and analysis 148 framework for hantaviruses. 149 150 Establishment of whole hantavirus segment amplification. While amplification 151 of the S and M segments in single amplicons has been achieved before, capturing the 152 entire L segment in one single amplicon has so far proven difficult (10). We utilized the 153 extremely high sequence conservation in the terminal 14 nucleotides of the 5’ and 3’ 154 ends of all three genome segments across the entire Orthohantavirus genus to design 155 universal hantavirus reverse transcription primers for both genomic negative-sense viral 156 RNA (vRNA) and the antigenomic positive-sense complementary RNA (cRNA) (Fig. 157 2A). Primers for amplification of individual segments also contained these highly 158 conserved termini but stretched further into the segments to achieve high specificity for 159 virus species and segments. 160 We established and optimised our virus species- and segment-specific viral genome 161 segment RT-PCR (vgsRT-PCR) method on RNA extracted from a cell-free purified 162 PUUV stock. First, we compared different RT primers and found that the Uni-c14 163 primer, random hexamers and oligo(dT) primers performed poorly and resulted in low or 164 no detectable amplification of PUUV segments (Fig. 2B). This was an expected result, 165 since hantaviruses generally are not thought to contain polyadenylation signals and 166 since the virus stock primarily should be composed of vRNA (14, 15). However, use of 167 5 the vRNA-specific Uni-v14 primer alone or in combination with the cRNA-specific Uni- 168 c14 primer yielded strong full-length amplification of all three PUUV segments. 169 Henceforth, the combination of vRNA- and cRNA-specific RT primers was used. Next, 170 different PCR elongation times and cycle numbers were compared. We observed that 171 for the longer L and M segments, increasing elongation time seemed to slightly increase 172 full-length segment amplification, while no major difference was observed for the S 173 segment (Fig. 2C). Based on these data we selected an elongation time of 3 min as the 174 best balance between sensitivity and overall reaction time. Increasing PCR cycle 175 numbers steadily increased PCR product accumulation in all three segments, with 176 robust product accumulation starting at 30 cycles (Fig 2D). As a compromise between 177 sensitivity, PCR bias and time optimisation, we chose 30 cycles as our default option, 178 with the possibility of increasing cycles to 40 for samples that require higher sensitivity. 179 As a proof-of-concept we also tested whether all segment-specific primers can be 180 combined in a single reaction and confirmed that all PUUV segments were efficiently 181 and equally amplified compared to the single primer pair reactions (Fig. 2E). Sensitivity 182 is important when designing PCR protocols for hantaviruses due to their inherently low 183 RNA copy numbers in infected patients. Using in vitro transcribed PUUV S segment 184 vRNA as a standard, we were able to accurately detect up to 101 RNA copies by RT- 185 qPCR (Fig. 2F) and up to 103 RNA copies by vgsRT-PCR (Fig. 2G). 186 Overall, we established a reproducible and sensitive vgsRT-PCR method for the optimal 187 amplification of whole PUUV segments with a single primer pair per segment. 188 189 Nanopore sequencing of diverse PUUV strains from cell culture. Having 190 established that we can robustly amplify full-length PUUV genomes, we next attempted 191 to sequence and characterise these amplicons from more complex samples by ONT 192 long-read sequencing. To that end, we infected human lung epithelial cells with several 193 different PUUV strains and extracted RNA from infected cells. First, we confirmed and 194 compared the presence of viral RNA by RT-qPCR and found robust – but varying – 195 levels of viral RNA in all samples (Fig.3A). Analysis of vgsRT-PCR products by gel 196 electrophoresis demonstrated clean amplification of the full M and S segments for all 197 PUUV strains (Fig. 3B). However, for the L segment we predominantly observed PCR 198 products of varying shorter lengths, suggesting production of internally truncated DVGs 199 that maintained the conserved segment termini. This was especially pronounced for the 200 PUUV strain BE/Cg/Villers-la-Tour/1/2009 (‘Villers-la-Tour’), BE/Cg/Seloignes/1/2009 201 (‘Seloignes’), BE/Cg/Beaumont/1/2012 (‘Beaumont’), and BE/Cg/Turnhout/1/1985 202 (‘Turnhout’), while RUS/Cg/Kazan/E6/1982 (‘Kazan-E6’) exhibited relatively clean full- 203 length products. Interestingly, while these putative DVGs exhibited strain-specific 204 profiles, the overall size distribution appears similar across all virus strains. 205 Nanopore sequencing of these amplicons demonstrated high levels of sequencing 206 depth across the entire genome (Table 1 and Fig. 3C). The genome coverage was even 207 across the entire genome for the M and S segments for all PUUV strains, confirming our 208 previous vgsRT-PCR data. Accordingly, we observed a striking reduction in genome 209 coverage in the central regions of the L segment for all strains except Kazan-E6, which 210 also did not generate any major truncated PCR products. We used the ORCHID 211 pipeline to classify sequenced viral reads and confirmed our vgsRT-PCR and genome 212 6 coverage data: while the M and S segments only contained small fractions of putative 213 and high-confidence DVGs, the vast majority of L segment reads were classified as 214 delVGs (Table 1 and Fig. 3D). Only Kazan-E6 exhibited a lower – yet still significant – 215 fraction of DVGs, consistent with our previous findings. As the M and S segments did 216 not exhibit any meaningful levels of DVGs, and cbVGs could not be detected at 217 significant levels in any segment, we characterized only L segment delVGs further. 218 Analysis of L segment delVG junction sizes revealed a now familiar pattern: while 219 Kazan-E6 only showed few unique junctions that were concentrated between 3000 and 220 4000 nt in size, all the remaining strains almost exclusively had very large 221 (approximately 4000 to 6000 nt in size) deletions (Fig. 3E). This helps explain why we 222 previously observed a relatively uniform pattern of truncated PCR products (Fig. 3B). 223 Investigation of the exact junction sites – i.e. at what nucleotide position of the genome 224 the RdRp disengages from the template (junction start) and then subsequently 225 reengages again (junction end) – helps shed further light onto the nature of these DVGs 226 and reveals highly specific regions in the PUUV L segment that are associated with 227 delVG formation (Fig. 3F). For the Turnhout, Beaumont, Seloignes and Villers-la-Tour 228 strains we observed highly similar patterns: the majority of deletions start within the first 229 100 nt of the 5’ end of the L segment and span almost the entire segment and end 230 within a more variable (approximately 1500 nt) window at the 3’ end of the segment 231 (Fig.3F). 232 Together, these data demonstrated that our whole segment amplicon sequencing 233 method is able to robustly sequence and resolve entire PUUV genomes. In addition, our 234 analysis framework allows us to confidently call and characterise DVGs from nanopore 235 sequencing data, identifying high abundance delVGs in most PUUV L segments. 236 237 Sequencing of PUUV geno…

full_text_sections.full_text: 1 An ONT sequencing framework for hantavirus genome assembly, 1 variant analysis, and defective viral genome characterization from 2 whole-segment amplicons 3 4 Léna Vandenabeele1, Frances M. Twohig2, Anne Tuiskunen Bäck3,4,5,6, Magnus 5 Sjöblom7, Rebecca Lantto3, Gabriella Svala7, Janne Tynell8,9, Sandra Broddesson10,11, 6 Robert Dyrdak10,11, Wanda Christ1, Silke Riesle-Sbarbaro12, Joseph B. Prescott12, 7 Steven B. Bradfute2, Daniel P. Depledge13,14,15, Benjamin E. Nilsson-Payant1 8 9 1 Division of Virology and Immunology, Department of Microbiology, Tumor and Cell 10 Biology, Karolinska Institutet, Stockholm, Sweden 11 2 Department of Internal Medicine, Center for Global Health, University of New Mexico 12 Health Sciences Center, Albuquerque, New Mexico, United States of America 13 3 Department of Clinical Microbiology, Umeå University, Umeå, Sweden 14 4 Department of Public Health and Clinical Medicine, Umeå University, Umeå, Sweden 15 5 Umeå Centre for Microbial Research (UCMR), Umeå University, Umeå, Sweden 16 6 Laboratory for Molecular Infection Medicine Sweden (MIMS), Umeå University, Umeå, 17 Sweden 18 7 Clinical Microbiology Unit, Department of Laboratory Medicine, Sunderby Hospital, 19 Luleå, Sweden 20 8 Department of Virology, University of Helsinki, Helsinki, Finland 21 9 Institute of Biomedicine, University of Turku, Turku, Finland 22 10 Division of Clinical Genomics & Virology, Department of Microbiology, Tumor and Cell 23 Biology, Karolinska Institutet, Stockholm, Sweden 24 11 Department of Clinical Microbiology, Karolinska University Hospital, Stockholm, 25 Sweden 26 12 Center for Biological Threats and Special Pathogens, Robert Koch Institute, Berlin, 27 Germany 28 13 Institute of Virology, Hannover Medical School, Hannover, Germany 29 14 Cluster of Excellence RESIST (EXC 2155), Hannover Medical School, Hannover 30 Germany 31 15 German Center for Infection Research (DZIF), partner site Hannover-Braunschweig, 32 Hannover, Germany 33 34 35 Corresponding author: benjamin.nilssonpayant@ki.se 36 37 38 39 40 2 ABSTRACT 41 Orthohantaviruses are zoonotic, tri-segmented negative-sense RNA viruses of rodents 42 and other small mammals that can cause severe human disease. Whole genome 43 sequencing remains difficult because of low viral loads, high sequence diversity, and an 44 inherent instability of the viral L segment. Current tiled amplicon and hybrid-capture 45 approaches do not capture the heterogeneity of virus populations, including defective 46 viral genomes (DVGs), which have never been described for hantaviruses. Here, we 47 present an Oxford Nanopore Technologies sequencing framework based on universal 48 reverse transcription primers targeting the conserved genome termini of 49 orthohantaviruses and a single species-specific primer pair per segment, enabling 50 amplification and sequencing of complete S, M, and L segments. We also developed an 51 accompanying bioinformatic pipeline that performs reference-guided assembly of 52 hantavirus genomes, consensus generation, variant calling, and DVG classification 53 using the newly developed ORCHID classification pipeline. We applied this approach to 54 diverse Puumala virus strains from infected cell cultures and bank voles, to 55 representative Old World and New World orthohantaviruses, and to highly pathogenic 56 New World viruses in vivo. In all cases we were able to accurately reconstruct full 57 hantavirus genomes. Notably, we found that hantavirus populations contain highly 58 abundant DVGs and conserved L segment deletions, whereas the S and M segments 59 remained largely intact. Together, this work provides a low-cost, broadly applicable and 60 easily customisable workflow for hantavirus genomics and reveals DVGs as a 61 previously unrecognized feature of hantavirus populations. 62 63 IMPORTANCE 64 Hantaviruses cause severe and often fatal human diseases, and their diversity and low 65 viral loads make them hard to sequence, which limits surveillance and outbreak 66 investigation. We describe a simple, universal but customisable, low-cost nanopore 67 sequencing workflow that recovers complete genome segments, including the full-length 68 L segment, from cell culture and animal tissues across the entire Orthohantavirus 69 genus. Using this approach, we report the first evidence of defective viral genomes in 70 hantaviruses. These truncated genomes arise mainly from the L segment, which 71 encodes the viral polymerase, and are formed at conserved genomic regions. Defective 72 viral genomes can modulate viral replication, innate immune activation, and persistence 73 in other viruses. Their presence in hantaviruses raises new questions about polymerase 74 function, tolerance in reservoir hosts, and immune-mediated disease in humans. Our 75 framework offers a practical tool for hantavirus genomics and a foundation for 76 investigating how defective genomes shape hantavirus infection. 77 3 INTRODUCTION 78 Orthohantaviruses (family Hantaviridae, class Bunyaviricetes) are zoonotic segmented 79 negative-sense RNA viruses that are naturally found in small mammal species, 80 including rodents, shrews, moles and bats (1). Human infections occur primarily through 81 inhalation of aerosolized excreta from infected animal hosts and can cause severe 82 disease, including haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and nephropathia 83 epidemica (NE) caused by Old World hantaviruses primarily in Eurasia and hantavirus 84 cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) caused by New World hantaviruses in the Americas 85 (2, 3). Case fatality rates for hantavirus diseases vary significantly depending on the 86 infecting virus species (4): it ranges from <1% for Puumala virus (PUUV), the causative 87 agent for NE, to up to 15% for HFRS-causing Old World hantaviruses such as Hantaan 88 virus (HTNV) in East Asia and Dobrava-Belgrade virus (DOBV) in eastern Europe, and 89 over 30% for HCPS-causing New World hantaviruses such as Andes virus (ANDV) and 90 Sin Nombre virus (SNV). 91 Hantaviruses have small tripartite negative-sense RNA genomes comprising the small 92 (S), medium (M) and large (L) genome segments, encoding only 4-5 viral proteins (5). 93 The S segment encodes the nucleoprotein (NP) and in some cases a non-structural 94 (NS) protein, the M segment encodes the glycoprotein precursor (GPC) which is co- 95 translationally cleaved into the Gn and Gc glycoproteins, and the L segment encodes 96 the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp). The genetic sequence divergence at the 97 amino acid level is significant across the hantavirus family (up to 75%) and even within 98 a species (up to 24%) (6). Low viral RNA copy numbers in clinical and rodent samples, 99 and natural RNA degradation outside of infected hosts makes obtaining complete 100 coverage of hantavirus genomes challenging (7, 8). Current state-of-the-art sequencing 101 approaches include metagenome sequencing, tiled amplicon sequencing and hybrid 102 capture-based sequencing, which all require extensive optimisation and large numbers 103 of probes (9–12). Existing long-read amplicon-based sequencing approaches often 104 include single amplicons for the smaller segments, but to date, there are no established 105 protocols to reliably capture the entire L segment in a single amplicon. In addition, while 106 these methods can provide full genome coverage sequencing and provide consensus 107 sequences of viruses, they do not accurately reflect the genetic makeup of any given 108 virus population. In reality, virus populations are highly heterogeneous and contain large 109 proportions of defective viral genomes (DVGs) consisting of genome truncations, 110 duplications and recombinations (13). However, DVGs have so far never been reported 111 for hantaviruses. 112 Here, we designed a whole segment amplicon-based long-read nanopore sequencing 113 method and an end-to-end bioinformatical analysis pipeline for hantavirus genome 114 assembly, alignment, consensu…

analysis.summary_en: Background: Orthohantaviruses cause severe disease and are hard to sequence due to low loads and L‑segment instability. Methods: An ONT workflow with universal RT primers and a species‑specific primer pair per segment, plus a reference‑guided bioinformatic pipeline, was applied to diverse hantavirus strains from culture and animal samples. Results: Full genomes were accurately reconstructed; abundant DVGs, especially L‑segment deletions, were identified—the first evidence of DVGs in hantaviruses. analysis_zh.background: 正汉坦病毒是鼠类及其他小型哺乳动物的动物源性、三段负链RNA病毒,可导致严重的人类疾病 (A1)。全基因组测序受限于病毒载量低、序列多样性高以及L段不稳定等因素 (A2)。
analysis_zh.methods: 作者开发了一套基于Oxford Nanopore Technologies的工作流程,使用针对保守基因组末端的通用逆转录引物以及每个基因组片段的单一物种特异性引物对,以扩增完整的S、M和L段 (A4)。随附的参考导向生物信息学管线实现组装、共识序列生成、变异检测以及缺陷病毒基因组(DVG)分类 (A5)。该方法已应用于来自细胞培养、田鼠、代表性旧世界和新世界正汉坦病毒以及体内高度致病的新世界病毒的多样普马拉病毒株系 (A6)。
analysis_zh.results: 在所有检测样本中均准确重建了完整的汉坦病毒基因组 (A7)。作者发现汉坦病毒群体中存在大量DVG,尤其是L段的保守缺失,而S段和M段基本保持完整 (A8)。这为汉坦病毒中DVG的存在提供了首次证据 (A12)。
analysis_zh.contribution: 该工作流程提供了一种低成本、适用范围广且易于定制的汉坦病毒基因组学工具,覆盖整个属 (A9)。通过实现完整基因组片段(包括全长L段)的回收,提升了监测和疫情调查能力 (A10)。DVG的鉴定为研究其对聚合酶功能、宿主耐受性及免疫介导疾病的潜在影响开辟了新途径 (A13)。
analysis_zh.limitations: 限制未在提供的证据中报告。

papers.title: Can Hantavirus cruise into the next pandemic?
papers.abstract: Despite concerns arising from a recent ship-associated outbreak on the M/V Hondius cruise, current evidence suggests that Andes virus (ANDV) poses a low pandemic risk. Nevertheless, viral evolution, ecological changes, and reservoir host dynamics could drive future emergence of ANDV, underscoring the need for improved surveillance, diagnostics, therapeutics, and vaccine preparedness.

papers.title: Vaccines Against Hantavirus Infections: A Systematic Literature Review.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Hantaviruses infections are responsible for a hemorrhagic fever with renal and cardiopulmonary syndrome with case-fatality rates up to 50%. While inactivated vaccines are already available in China and South Korea, several additional candidate vaccines are under development. This systematic review summarizes the current clinical evidence on immunogenicity and short-term safety of vaccines targeting different hantavirus strains. Methods: Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, a systematic literature search was carried out to identify randomized and nonrandomized trials of any phase. Data were synthesized narratively within strata defined by vaccine platform, target virus, assay, immunogenicity and safety. Results: Ten trials on 961 adults were included: four single-arm trials on the inactivated vaccine and six early-phase DNA-vaccine trials. One month after last dose, the inactivated vaccine achieved neutralizing seropositivity by PRNT50 in 45.1% of the tested subjects after two priming doses and 55.7% after three, while the corresponding binding-antibody values measured by IFA were 87.3% and 95.7%. Among DNA vaccines, homologous responses reached 100% against HTNV and 83.3% against PUUV with monovalent constructs, whereas dual responses to the bivalent construct were registered in 33.3% and 77.8% of the subjects, when measured through PRNT50 and PsVNA50, respectively. One serious adverse event occurred, most likely unrelated to vaccination. Conclusions: No serious safety signal was identified, although safety remains insufficiently characterized. Measured immunogenicity depends as much on the assay as on the vaccine, and, in the absence of a validated correlate of protection, it cannot be read as a clinical benefit. Future research should prioritize validated correlates of protection and innovative trial designs adapted to low-incidence diseases.

Gaps: Safety is insufficiently characterized and no validated correlate of protection exists (A10, A11). Future research: Prioritize validated correlates and innovative low‑incidence trial designs (A12).

papers.title: Rising spillover risk: Lessons from the Andes hantavirus outbreak.
papers.abstract: The unprecedented expansion of human activity boundaries is turning spillover from a chance event into a foreseeable ecological and epidemiological certainty. Using the 2026 Andes hantavirus cruise ship outbreak as an entry point, this study examines it within a broader driver framework: nearly all emerging infectious disease events in humans in recent decades have originated from wildlife transmission; under climate-change and land-use scenarios, approximately 3139 mammal species are projected to aggregate in new combinations by 2070, causing an estimated 4000 cross-species viral transmission events. The rapid expansion of tourism into ecologically fragile regions - sub-Antarctic waters, the deep sea, and primary forests - the persistence of habitat fragmentation and animal trade, and the reshaping of wildlife distribution and vector dynamics by extreme climate events together constitute "novel contact amplifiers" that accelerate contact at the human-animal-environment interface. Robotics, artificial intelligence, autonomous driving, and automated logistics are extending human activities into previously inaccessible regions, yet they remain almost entirely absent from current spillover risk assessments. The limitations of cruise ship medical systems - whose core capacity lies in "recognize, isolate, stabilize, and transfer" rather than definitive diagnosis and treatment - were fully exposed in this event. From a One Health perspective, this paper proposes that responses to spillover risk must shift from passive reaction to proactive interface governance, incorporate technology-driven increases in contact frequency into prevention and control frameworks, and advance cornerstone strategies such as broad-spectrum vaccines and broad-spectrum antiviral drugs at the basic research level.

Methods: Using the 2026 Andes hantavirus cruise‑ship outbreak as an entry point, the study examines it within a broader driver framework linking wildlife transmission to emerging infectious diseases. papers.title_zh: 上升的溢出风险:安第斯病毒 汉坦病毒 爆发的经验教训。

analysis_zh.background: 前所未有的人类活动边界扩张正把偶发的溢出事件转变为可预见的生态和流行病学必然。
analysis_zh.methods: 以2026年安第斯病毒 汉坦病毒 邮轮暴发为切入点,研究在更广泛的驱动因素框架下,将野生动物传播与新发传染病联系起来进行考察。
analysis_zh.results: 在气候变化和土地利用情景下,预计到2070年约有3,139种哺乳动物将以新组合聚集,导致约4,000起跨物种病毒传播事件。
analysis_zh.contribution: 本文指出了新型接触放大因素——旅游、栖息地碎片化、动物贸易以及气候驱动的野生动物迁移——加速了人‐动物‐环境接触,并呼吁采取主动的“一体健康”治理以及研发广谱疫苗和抗病毒药物。
analysis_zh.limitations: 机器人、人工智能、自动驾驶和自动化物流将人类活动延伸至先前不可及的地区,但在当前的溢出风险评估中几乎完全缺失。

papers.title: Differential PCDH1 usage by Laguna Negra and Black Creek Canal hantaviruses.
papers.abstract: UNLABELLED: Laguna Negra virus and Black Creek Canal virus are hantaviruses associated with hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), but their cellular entry receptors have not been defined. We used replication-competent recombinant vesicular stomatitis viruses (rVSVs) bearing hantavirus Gn/Gc glycoprotein complexes to compare entry by these viruses, the Old World rodent-borne Dabieshan virus and Tigray virus, and the shrew-borne Cao Bang virus and Amga virus. All six Gn/Gc complexes supported infection of primary human pulmonary microvascular endothelial cells, with virus-specific efficiencies and kinetics. Genetic ablation of protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) reduced infection mediated by Laguna Negra virus and Black Creek Canal virus Gn/Gc in human osteosarcoma and endothelial cells, whereas PCDH1 re-expression restored susceptibility. Both viruses were captured by a soluble PCDH1 protein comprising the first two extracellular cadherin domains. Infection was also inhibited by a soluble decoy containing the first cadherin domain, and by an antibody specific to that domain, indicating that the first PCDH1 cadherin domain mediates viral engagement. Black Creek Canal Gn/Gc-bearing rVSVs incorporated less Gn/Gc and showed lower apparent capture by PCDH1 than Laguna Negra virus and Andes virus Gn/Gc-bearing particles, even after normalization for glycoprotein abundance. In contrast, PCDH1 depletion did not detectably alter infection mediated by the other four hantavirus Gn/Gc complexes. Thus, Laguna Negra virus and Black Creek Canal virus use PCDH1 for efficient entry but differ in apparent receptor engagement and responses to PCDH1-directed inhibitors, whereas all six viruses are potently neutralized by the broadly reactive Gn/Gc-directed antibody ADI-42898. IMPORTANCE: The receptors used by many medically important hantaviruses remain incompletely characterized. Using BSL2-compatible rVSVs bearing hantavirus glycoproteins, we show that Laguna Negra virus and Black Creek Canal virus, two hantaviruses associated with human cardiopulmonary disease, used protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) for efficient entry into human cells. PCDH1-directed inhibitors blocked infection, but the two viruses differed in apparent receptor engagement and inhibitor sensitivity, showing that PCDH1 usage is not uniform even among closely related viruses. Gn/Gc complexes from four additional divergent hantaviruses carried by shrews and Old World rodents infected primary human endothelial cells without detectable PCDH1 dependence, emphasizing the need to identify alternative entry factors. A broadly reactive antibody neutralized every virus in the study panel, supporting conserved viral glycoprotein surfaces as therapeutic targets when receptor usage is diverse or unknown.

Results: PCDH1 ablation reduced infection by Laguna Negra and Black Creek Canal; re‑expression restored susceptibility; soluble PCDH1 captured the viruses; a decoy and antibody against the first cadherin domain inhibited infection; Black Creek Canal showed lower capture and inhibitor sensitivity; other hantaviruses were PCDH1‑independent. Contribution: The study shows differential PCDH1 usage among closely related hantaviruses, identifies alternative entry factors for other viruses, and demonstrates a broadly reactive antibody that neutralizes all tested viruses. Limitations: not reported in the supplied evidence.

papers.title: Blood Metabolites as Biomarkers and Metabolism Mechanism Studies of Hemorrhagic Fever With Renal Syndrome.
papers.abstract: Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS) is a potentially life-threatening hantavirus zoonosis endemic to East Asia, especially China, featuring fever, hemorrhage, and acute renal injury. This study aimed to identify serum metabolic biomarkers for HFRS staging and explore impaired metabolic pathways. We performed untargeted serum metabolomic profiling via ultra-performance liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry (UPLC-MS/MS) on samples from acute-phase, convalescent HFRS patients, and healthy controls. Data from untargeted metabolomics showed that 168 metabolites were significantly altered in HFRS patients. Among these, 14 metabolites could distinguish the pairwise group comparisons (patient/NC, AP/CP, AP/NC, and CP/NC), with univariate AUCs ranging from 0.7556 to 1.000; a LASSO-based combined model yielded leave-one-out cross-validated (LOOCV) AUCs of 1.000, 0.993, and 0.840 for AP/NC, CP/NC, and AP/CP, respectively, indicating their potential to distinguish disease stages. Pathway analysis revealed significant perturbations in arginine biosynthesis, ascorbate and aldarate metabolism, and taurine and hypotaurine metabolism, indicating the importance in the metabolic dysfunction of HFRS. Metabolites within the arginine biosynthesis pathway were markedly altered and effectively differentiated acute-phase HFRS from healthy controls, suggesting their role in predicting acute disease status. Distinct serum metabolite abundance shifts can stratify HFRS stages. The 14 metabolites and their combined panels discriminated disease stages with univariate AUCs of 0.756-1.000 and leave-one-out cross-validated AUCs of 0.840-1.000, supporting serum metabolites as candidate biomarkers for distinguishing HFRS stages and providing a basis for targeted metabolomics studies of HFRS.

papers.title_zh: 血液代谢物作为生物标志物及 肾综合征出血热 的代谢机制研究。

analysis_zh.background: 肾综合征出血热(HFRS)是一种潜在危及生命的汉坦病毒人畜共患病,流行于东亚,尤其是中国,表现为发热、出血和急性肾损伤。
analysis_zh.methods: 采用超高效液相色谱-串联质谱(UPLC‐MS/MS)进行的非靶向血清代谢组学分析,对急性期、恢复期肾综合征出血热(HFRS)患者及健康对照的样本进行检测。
analysis_zh.results: 共检测到168种代谢物显著变化;其中14种代谢物可区分患者组,单变量AUC为0.7556–1.000;基于LASSO的组合模型在留一交叉验证中得到AUC为1.000(急性期/健康对照),0.993(恢复期/健康对照)和0.840(急性期/恢复期)。
analysis_zh.contribution: 这些代谢物及其组合面板构成区分肾综合征出血热疾病阶段的候选血清生物标志物,并揭示精氨酸、抗坏血酸和牛磺酸代谢通路的紊乱,为进一步机制研究提供线索。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅提供摘要数据;样本量、人口学信息、地理位置及外部验证均未报告。

papers.title: Andes virus reaches Europe: a narrative review on clinical challenges, diagnostic gaps and public health preparedness, 2026.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND Up to 2 July 2026, a total of 13 cases of Andes virus (ANDV) including three deaths were reported in connection to an outbreak on the cruise ship m/v Hondius , which departed from Argentina in April and subsequently travelled to Europe to evacuate the passengers. This event prompted all European health authorities to take action to limit the spread of the virus. AIM To synthesise current knowledge on ANDV, with particular attention on laboratory diagnosis and capability gaps. METHODS A literature search on ANDV was conducted, with a focus on human infection, transmission, outbreak investigations, countermeasures and diagnostics. To provide context for the ship-linked outbreak, updates from official public health sources, including the World Health Organization and European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control were used. Moreover, activities by European Union Public Health Reference Laboratories for Emerging, Rodent-borne and Zoonotic Viral Pathogens (EURL-PH-ERZV) were briefly presented. RESULTS Andes virus is unique among hantaviruses because of sustained person-to-person transmission. Diagnosis relies on integration of clinical and epidemiological information with molecular detection of viral RNA or serological evidence. At the time of the outbreak, European diagnostic preparedness was generally well established, but important gaps remained prompting rapid support from the EURL-PH-ERZV. CONCLUSIONS The recent event demonstrated how a geographically restricted zoonotic infection can pose public health challenges beyond endemic areas. This highlights the need for strong collaboration between clinical services, public health authorities and reference laboratories to strengthen surveillance, early detection, risk assessment and diagnostic preparedness for emerging pathogens.

source_records.abstract: BACKGROUNDUp to 2 July 2026, a total of 13 cases of Andes virus (ANDV) including three deaths were reported in connection to an outbreak on the cruise ship m/v Hondius , which departed from Argentina in April and subsequently travelled to Europe to evacuate the passengers. This event prompted all European health authorities to take action to limit the spread of the virus.AIMTo synthesise current knowledge on ANDV, with particular attention on laboratory diagnosis and capability gaps.METHODSA literature search on ANDV was conducted, with a focus on human infection, transmission, outbreak investigations, countermeasures and diagnostics. To provide context for the ship-linked outbreak, updates from official public health sources, including the World Health Organization and European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control were used. Moreover, activities by European Union Public Health Reference Laboratories for Emerging, Rodent-borne and Zoonotic Viral Pathogens (EURL-PH-ERZV) were briefly presented.RESULTSAndes virus is unique among hantaviruses because of sustained person-to-person transmission. Diagnosis relies on integration of clinical and epidemiological information with molecular detection of viral RNA or serological evidence. At the time of the outbreak, European diagnostic preparedness was generally well established, but important gaps remained prompting rapid support from the EURL-PH-ERZV.CONCLUSIONSThe recent event demonstrated how a geographically restricted zoonotic infection can pose public health challenges beyond endemic areas. This highlights the need for strong collaboration between clinical services, public health authorities and reference laboratories to strengthen surveillance, early detection, risk assessment and diagnostic preparedness for emerging pathogens.

analysis.background: The review was prompted by a 2026 outbreak of Andes virus (ANDV) on the cruise ship m/v Hondius, which resulted in 13 cases and three deaths after the vessel traveled from Argentina to Europe (A1) and led European health authorities to act (A2).
analysis.main_directions: It synthesises current knowledge on ANDV with emphasis on its unique sustained person‑to‑person transmission (A7), clinical and epidemiological diagnosis integrating molecular and serological methods (A8), diagnostic capability gaps (A9), and the role of reference laboratories and inter‑sectoral collaboration (A11).
analysis.current_state: ANDV is the only hantavirus known for sustained human‑to‑human spread (A7); diagnosis relies on combined clinical, epidemiological, molecular and serological data (A8); and European diagnostic preparedness was generally established though imperfect (A9).
analysis.gaps: Important diagnostic and surveillance gaps remained during the outbreak (A9), and coordination among clinical services, public health authorities and reference labs is still insufficient (A11).
analysis.future_research: Future work should strengthen collaborative networks to enhance surveillance, early detection, risk assessment and diagnostic preparedness for emerging zoonoses like ANDV (A11).

analysis.summary_en: Background: An outbreak of Andes virus on a cruise ship traveling from Argentina to Europe in 2026, with 13 cases and three deaths, prompted European health authorities to review preparedness. Main directions: The review focuses on ANDV's unique sustained person‑to‑person transmission, integrated clinical/epidemiological diagnosis, diagnostic capability gaps, and the need for collaboration among labs and public health. Current state: ANDV is the only hantavirus with documented sustained human‑to‑human spread; diagnosis combines clinical, epidemiological, molecular and serological data; European diagnostic capacity was broadly in place. Gaps: Diagnostic and surveillance gaps persisted during the outbreak, and coordination between clinical services, public health and reference laboratories remains inadequate. Future research: Strengthen collaborative networks to improve surveillance, early detection, risk assessment and diagnostic preparedness for emerging zoonoses like ANDV.

papers.title_zh: 安第斯病毒进入欧洲:关于临床挑战、诊断缺口与公共卫生准备的叙述性综述,2026年。

analysis_zh.background: 该综述的动因是2026年在邮轮 m/v Hondius 上爆发的 安第斯病毒(ANDV),该船从阿根廷航行至欧洲期间导致13例感染和3例死亡 (A1),并促使欧洲卫生当局采取行动 (A2)。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 本文综合了关于 ANDV 的最新认识,重点强调其独特的持续人际传播 (A7)、融合分子与血清学方法的临床与流行病学诊断 (A8)、诊断能力缺口 (A9),以及参考实验室和跨部门协作的作用 (A11)。
analysis_zh.current_state: ANDV 是唯一已知能够持续人际传播的 汉坦病毒(A7);诊断依赖临床、流行病学、分子和血清学数据的综合 (A8);欧洲的诊断准备总体已建立,但仍不完善 (A9)。
analysis_zh.gaps: 在此次暴发期间仍存在重要的诊断和监测缺口 (A9),且临床服务、公共卫生部门与参考实验室之间的协作仍显不足 (A11)。
analysis_zh.future_research: 未来工作应加强协作网络,以提升对包括 ANDV 在内的新发人畜共患病的监测、早期发现、风险评估和诊断准备 (A11)。
